items.q: According to the Euro Ewing 2012 randomised trial (Brennan et al., Lancet 2022), which induction chemotherapy regimen demonstrated superior event-free and overall survival with lower toxicity compared to the VIDE regimen for Ewing sarcoma?
o: Interval-compressed VDC/IE (vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide, etoposide every 2 weeks)
items.e: The Euro Ewing 2012 trial established interval-compressed VDC/IE (administered every 2 weeks) as superior to the European VIDE induction regimen in both event-free and overall survival, making it the transatlantic standard of care. Standard osteosarcoma regimens like MAP or rhabdomyosarcoma regimens like VAC are not used for Ewing sarcoma.
items.note: Accurate trial-based oncology question matching current standard guidelines.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy undergoes wide resection of a diaphyseal femoral Ewing sarcoma following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. On histopathological assessment of the resected specimen, which threshold defines a poor histological response?
items.e: In Ewing sarcoma, a poor histological response is defined as 10% or more viable tumour cells remaining in the specimen (less than 90% necrosis). A poor histological response is an established adverse prognostic factor and may prompt postoperative radiotherapy or consideration of intensified consolidation.
items.note: Standard histological response threshold across orthopaedic oncology.

items.q: In multiple myeloma, skeletal lesions appear purely osteolytic on plain radiographs and are characteristically 'cold' (false negative) on technetium-99m bone scintigraphy primarily because:
o: Extensive local microvascular thrombosis prevents radiotracer delivery to the bone marrow
Excessive osteoprotegerin (OPG) secretion suppresses osteoclastic bone resorption
Malignant plasma cells produce direct enzymatic dissolution of mineralised matrix without cytokine signaling
Tumour cells secrete DKK1 and sclerostin, causing potent suppression of osteoblastic bone formation
items.e: Myeloma cells upregulate RANKL to activate osteoclasts and secrete DKK1 and sclerostin to inhibit osteoblasts. The profound absence of osteoblastic bone repair explains why the lesions are purely lytic without reactive sclerosis, alkaline phosphatase remains normal, and bone scintigraphy is characteristically false-negative.
items.note: Classic pathophysiology question on myeloma bone destruction mechanism.

items.q: A 52-year-old male presents with deep thigh pain. Radiographs show a permeative lytic lesion of the femoral diaphysis with minimal periosteal reaction. MRI reveals extensive intramedullary replacement with a large soft-tissue mass surrounding a relatively preserved cortex. Core needle biopsy demonstrates diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (CD45 and CD20 positive). Staging PET-CT confirms localized bone lymphoma without nodal or visceral disease. What is the definitive management of the tumour?
o: Systemic chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP) with or without consolidation radiotherapy
Wide en bloc diaphyseal segmental resection with endoprosthetic reconstruction
Extended intralesional curettage, liquid nitrogen cryotherapy, and cement augmentation
Above-knee amputation followed by local field radiotherapy
items.e: Primary bone lymphoma is treated definitively with systemic chemoimmunotherapy (such as R-CHOP) with or without consolidation radiotherapy. Surgery has no oncological role in tumour resection; orthopaedic interventions are limited to biopsy and stabilization of impending or established pathological fractures.
items.note: Clear, standard management paradigm for primary lymphoma of bone.

items.q: A 16-year-old adolescent presents with a deep, rapidly growing forearm mass. Biopsy demonstrates sheets of small round blue cells with positive immunohistochemical staining for desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1, consistent with alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Which chromosomal translocation is characteristic of this tumour?
items.e: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is classically characterised by the t(2;13) PAX3-FOXO1 translocation (or less commonly t(1;13) PAX7-FOXO1). In contrast, t(11;22)(q24;q12) is hallmark of Ewing sarcoma, and t(11;22)(p13;q12) occurs in desmoplastic small round cell tumour.
items.note: High-yield cytogenetics question testing distinctions among small round cell tumours.

items.q: A 54-year-old man presents with localized thoracic spine pain. Imaging identifies an isolated lytic lesion of the T9 vertebral body without other lesions on whole-body low-dose CT. Biopsy reveals clonal CD138-positive plasma cells. Bone marrow aspirate shows under 5% plasma cells, and laboratory workup reveals normal serum calcium, normal creatinine, and no anaemia. Which statement regarding solitary plasmacytoma of bone is correct?
o: En bloc spondylectomy is recommended as the definitive first-line oncological treatment
Definitive local radiotherapy (40–50 Gy) is the standard treatment of choice
Less than 10% of cases progress to multiple myeloma within 10 years
Serum alkaline phosphatase is characteristically markedly elevated
items.e: Solitary plasmacytoma of bone is highly radiosensitive, and definitive radiotherapy (40–50 Gy) achieves local control rates exceeding 85%. However, 50% to 70% of patients progress to systemic multiple myeloma within 10 years, necessitating prolonged clinical and biochemical surveillance.
items.note: Accurate, textbook-supported facts on solitary plasmacytoma.

items.q: On plain radiographs of a patient with vertebral collapse, preservation of the pedicles ('absent pedicle sign' is negative) characteristically favours multiple myeloma over osteolytic metastases because:
o: Plasma cells produce sclerostin that specifically protects posterior element cortical architecture
Metastatic carcinoma requires higher vascular flow found exclusively in the transverse processes
The pedicles contain comparatively little haematopoietic red marrow relative to the vertebral body
Myeloma cells are unable to penetrate through the posterior longitudinal ligament
items.e: Myeloma is a disease of haematopoietic marrow; because the vertebral body contains abundant red marrow while the pedicles contain predominantly fatty marrow, vertebral bodies are preferentially destroyed early while pedicles are characteristically spared. In contrast, metastatic carcinoma frequently seeds and destroys pedicles early (producing the 'winking owl' sign).
items.note: Classic diagnostic radiological sign and anatomical basis.

items.q: A 12-year-old girl sustains a pathological fracture through a previously unrecognised diaphyseal lesion of the femur. Biopsy confirms Ewing sarcoma without distant metastases on staging. What is the most appropriate initial orthopaedic management strategy?
o: Immediate intramedullary interlocking nailing to allow early weight-bearing
Non-operative immobilisation (splint or cast) followed by neoadjuvant induction chemotherapy
Emergency primary hip disarticulation because the fracture causes tumour contamination
Urgent local external beam radiotherapy to 55 Gy before starting systemic therapy
items.e: Pathological fracture at presentation in Ewing sarcoma is managed by initial non-operative immobilisation (splinting or casting) followed promptly by standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Internal fixation is strictly avoided as it contaminates the medullary canal and soft-tissue planes; successful limb salvage remains feasible after induction chemotherapy.
items.note: Essential clinical principle in paediatric orthopaedic oncology.

items.q: In general, soft-tissue sarcomas metastasise primarily via the haematogenous route, with lymph-node spread occurring in fewer than 5% of cases. Which of the following subtypes is classically recognized for having an increased propensity for lymph-node metastasis?
items.e: Regional lymph node metastasis is rare in soft-tissue sarcomas (under 5%) except in specific 'node-seeking' variants remembered by the mnemonic SCARE: Synovial sarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, and Epithelioid sarcoma.
items.note: Accurate, high-yield classic concept directly supported by the notes.

items.q: A 42-year-old man presents with an 8 cm deep mass in the anterior compartment of the thigh suspected to be a sarcoma. When performing an image-guided core needle biopsy of this extremity lesion, which of the following technical principles must be strictly adhered to?
o: The biopsy tract should traverse intermuscular planes to avoid muscle necrosis
A transverse skin incision should be used to follow relaxed skin tension lines
The biopsy must be oriented longitudinally and remain within a single anatomic compartment
Any surgical drain used must exit as far lateral and distant from the biopsy tract as possible
items.e: Biopsy of an extremity soft-tissue sarcoma must use a small longitudinal incision placed directly in line with the planned definitive resection, passing through a single compartment while strictly avoiding intermuscular planes, joints, and neurovascular bundles. Any drain must exit in line with and close to the incision so the entire tract can be excised en bloc.
items.note: Standard Mankin biopsy principles, fully accurate.

items.q: In the randomized controlled trial comparing preoperative radiotherapy (50 Gy) with postoperative radiotherapy (66 Gy) for extremity soft-tissue sarcoma (NCIC SR2 / O'Sullivan et al.), what was the principal finding regarding complications and outcomes?
o: Preoperative radiotherapy resulted in a significantly higher rate of major acute wound complications
Postoperative radiotherapy was associated with significantly lower rates of late fibrosis and joint stiffness
Preoperative radiotherapy produced a statistically significant improvement in overall survival
Postoperative radiotherapy yielded significantly superior local recurrence-free survival
items.e: The NCIC SR2 trial (O'Sullivan et al.) demonstrated equivalent local control and overall survival between both arms, but preoperative radiotherapy had a significantly higher incidence of major acute wound complications (about 35% vs 17%), while postoperative radiotherapy caused greater permanent late toxicities like subcutaneous fibrosis and joint stiffness.
items.note: Landmark trial accurately represented according to the notes.

items.q: A 30-year-old postpartum woman presents with an asymptomatic, biopsy-proven 6 cm desmoid-type fibromatosis of the anterior abdominal wall. According to the Desmoid Tumor Working Group consensus guidelines, what is the recommended initial management?
o: Immediate radical en bloc resection with 3 cm clear margins
Active surveillance with regular magnetic resonance imaging
Immediate combination cytotoxic chemotherapy with doxorubicin and ifosfamide
items.e: The Desmoid Tumor Working Group consensus establishes active surveillance with regular MRI as the first-line approach for asymptomatic or non-threatening desmoid fibromatosis, because these tumours never metastasise and a substantial proportion arrest or regress spontaneously.
items.note: Aligns precisely with standard updated guidelines in the notes.

items.q: A 38-year-old man undergoes core needle biopsy of a deep thigh mass demonstrating myxoid liposarcoma with the characteristic t(12;16)(q13;p11) translocation. When completing metastatic staging, which of the following is specifically indicated due to this subtype's distinct pattern of dissemination?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain
Bilateral lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound
items.e: Unlike most sarcomas that spread almost exclusively to the lungs, myxoid liposarcoma has a predilection for extrapulmonary metastatic sites, including the spine, retroperitoneum, and opposite extremity soft tissues, which are poorly seen on CT or PET and require whole-spine or whole-body MRI. Brain MRI staging is typically reserved for alveolar soft part sarcoma and angiosarcoma.
items.note: The draft had an answer-key mismatch (marked option C in draft despite the explanation explicitly arguing for option B). Fixed marked answer to index 1 (Option B).

items.q: The French Federation of Cancer Centers Sarcoma Group (FNCLCC) grading system is the standard histological grading system for soft-tissue sarcomas. All of the following parameters are scored to calculate the FNCLCC grade EXCEPT:
o: Depth relative to the deep investing fascia
items.e: The FNCLCC histological grading score is based strictly on three microscopic parameters: tumour differentiation (score 1-3), mitotic count (score 1-3), and tumour necrosis (score 0-2). Tumour depth is a clinical/staging parameter and is not a component of the FNCLCC histological grade.
items.note: Standard histological criteria question, technically flawless.

items.q: The landmark National Cancer Institute randomized trial by Rosenberg et al. (1982) established limb-sparing surgery as standard care in extremity soft-tissue sarcoma by demonstrating that:
o: Limb-sparing surgery combined with radiotherapy yielded equivalent overall survival compared to amputation
Amputation conferred a statistically significant overall survival benefit over limb salvage
Limb salvage alone resulted in a lower local recurrence rate than radical amputation
Postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy eliminated the need to obtain microscopically negative margins
items.e: Rosenberg et al. demonstrated that limb-sparing surgery combined with radiation therapy yielded equivalent overall survival compared to amputation, despite a small increase in local recurrence in the limb-sparing group, thereby establishing the oncological safety of limb salvage.
items.note: Historically pivotal trial in orthopaedic oncology, fully verified.

items.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging, painful mass in the popliteal fossa. Radiographs reveal focal soft-tissue calcification in approximately 30% of the tumour volume. Molecular testing demonstrates a t(X;18)(p11;q11) translocation producing an SS18-SSX fusion transcript. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Synovial sarcoma typically occurs in young adults (15-40 years) near large joints (especially around the knee/popliteal fossa), often presents with pain, shows soft-tissue calcification in about 30% of cases on radiographs, and is genetically defined by the t(X;18)(p11;q11) SS18-SSX translocation.
items.note: Classic presentation and genetics, completely sound.

items.q: A 62-year-old female presents with severe right groin pain when bearing weight. Radiographs demonstrate a purely lytic metastatic lesion measuring 4.5 cm in the peritrochanteric region of the right femur, occupying more than two-thirds of the cortical diameter. According to the Mirels scoring system, what is the score and the recommended management?
o: Score 10; radiotherapy and protected weight bearing
items.e: The Mirels score assigns 3 points for peritrochanteric location, 3 for functional/mechanical pain, 3 for a purely lytic lesion, and 3 for cortical diameter involvement exceeding two-thirds, yielding a total score of 12. A score of 9 or greater indicates a high fracture risk (≥33%) and warrants prophylactic surgical fixation.
items.note: Accurate application of Mirels criteria and management cut-off.

items.q: In the landmark randomised controlled trial by Patchell et al. (Lancet 2005) on metastatic spinal cord compression from solid tumours, what was the primary demonstrated benefit of surgical decompression and stabilization followed by radiotherapy compared with radiotherapy alone?
o: Significantly higher proportion of patients regaining or retaining the ability to walk
Complete elimination of the risk of local tumour recurrence in the vertebral column
Significantly reduced 30-day perioperative systemic morbidity and mortality
Superior long-term survival in patients presenting with radioresistant renal cell metastases
items.e: Patchell et al. demonstrated that direct circumferential decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy was superior to radiotherapy alone, with 84% versus 57% of patients able to walk after treatment, and non-ambulant patients regaining ambulation in 62% versus 19%.
items.note: High-yield landmark trial tested accurately according to primary outcomes.

items.q: A 58-year-old male presents with a solitary, painful osteolytic lesion in the proximal humerus with no prior cancer diagnosis. According to the diagnostic evaluation strategy described by Rougraff et al. (1993) for skeletal metastasis of unknown origin, which primary malignancy is most commonly identified?
items.e: In the Rougraff diagnostic protocol, a systematic workup (history, examination, basic labs, chest radiography, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and bone scintigraphy) identifies the primary in approximately 85% of cases, with non-small cell lung carcinoma being the most common unknown primary, followed by renal cell carcinoma.
items.note: Standard literature fact and classic exam question on metastasis of unknown origin.

items.q: According to the classic study by Gainor and Buchert (1983) evaluating the healing rates of pathological fractures secondary to metastatic skeletal disease, which primary malignancy had the poorest healing rate (essentially 0%)?
items.e: Gainor and Buchert demonstrated that fracture healing rates after pathological fractures vary dramatically by histology: myeloma was highest (~65-70%), followed by renal cell carcinoma (~45%), breast (~35-40%), and lung carcinoma essentially 0%.
items.note: Classic landmark finding regarding fracture healing in metastatic bone disease.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with disabling hip pain. Pelvic radiographs and CT demonstrate extensive periacetabular osteolysis with deficiency of the medial acetabular wall, but the superior acetabular dome and lateral cortices remain structurally intact. According to the Harrington classification of periacetabular metastases, what is the defect class and the standard reconstructive technique?
o: Class I; conventional cemented total hip arthroplasty
Class II; total hip arthroplasty with a protrusio cage/ring or mesh to transfer load to the intact rim
Class III; Harrington procedure utilizing Steinmann pins driven from the iliac crest with PMMA reinforcement
Class IV; wide en bloc resection followed by pelvic megaprosthetic replacement
items.e: Harrington Class II periacetabular defects are characterized by medial wall deficiency with intact lateral and superior walls. The standard reconstruction is a total hip arthroplasty supported by an antiprotrusio cage, ring, or mesh to bridge the defect and transmit loads to the intact peripheral cortical rim.
items.note: Accurate testing of Harrington classification and reconstructive options.

items.q: A 60-year-old male with prostate cancer presents with mid-back pain. Axial T2-weighted MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrates epidural metastatic extension causing spinal cord compression, but cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) remains clearly visible circumferentially around the cord. According to the Bilsky (Epidural Spinal Cord Compression - ESCC) grading scale, what is the grade of this lesion?
items.e: In the Bilsky ESCC grading system, Grade 2 represents spinal cord compression with CSF still visible around the cord. Grade 3 denotes high-grade spinal cord compression with complete obliteration of the CSF space.
items.note: Precise imaging-based classification question directly assessing Bilsky criteria.

items.q: Regarding the palliative radiotherapy regimens evaluated in the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study and RTOG 9714 for uncomplicated painful skeletal metastases, which statement correctly summarizes the trial conclusions?
o: Single-fraction 8 Gy provides equivalent pain relief to multifraction regimens but has a higher rate of retreatment
Multifraction regimens (e.g., 30 Gy in 10 fractions) achieve significantly higher overall pain response rates than 8 Gy
Single-fraction 8 Gy causes a significantly higher incidence of pathological fractures than multifraction regimens
Multifraction regimens are required to achieve meaningful remineralization and re-ossification of purely lytic lesions
items.e: Both RTOG 9714 and the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study confirmed that a single 8 Gy fraction delivers pain relief equivalent to multifraction courses (e.g., 30 Gy in 10 fractions or 20 Gy in 5 fractions), although the retreatment rate is significantly higher after a single fraction (~18-20% vs 8-10%).
items.note: Standard oncology clinical trial knowledge for orthopaedic oncology subspecialty exams.

items.q: A 56-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma reports mechanical lower back pain aggravated by standing and spinal loading. Imaging reveals a purely lytic metastatic lesion at T12 with 35% vertebral body collapse, intact posterolateral elements, and normal spinal alignment. What is his Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) and the corresponding mechanical stability category?
items.e: SINS assigns: Location T12 (junctional T11-L1) = 3; Pain (mechanical) = 3; Bone lesion (lytic) = 2; Alignment (normal) = 0; Vertebral collapse (<50%) = 2; Posterolateral involvement (none) = 0. Total score = 10 (3 + 3 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 0). A score between 7 and 12 denotes indeterminate (potentially unstable) spine disease, warranting surgical consultation.
items.note: Accurate SINS scoring computation and clinical categorization.

items.q: A 17-year-old male presents with persistent knee pain and swelling. Plain radiographs demonstrate an aggressive osteoblastic and osteolytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with a Codman triangle. What is the mandatory sequence of further workup before multidisciplinary team (MDT) review and treatment?
o: Local staging MRI of the whole involved bone, then systemic staging (CT chest and bone scan/PET-CT), then biopsy
Core needle biopsy, then local staging MRI of the whole tibia, then CT chest
CT chest and PET-CT, then open incisional biopsy, then local staging MRI of the tibia
Immediate open incisional biopsy, followed by CT chest, followed by local staging MRI of the proximal tibia
items.e: Biopsy must always be the final staging step because post-biopsy haematoma and peritumoral oedema distort MRI anatomy and artificially exaggerate tumour extent. The proper immutable sequence is plain radiography, local staging with MRI of the entire involved bone (to identify skip lesions), systemic staging (CT chest and bone scan/PET-CT), and finally a carefully planned biopsy at the treating sarcoma centre.
items.note: Accurate and tests an immutable tenet of musculoskeletal oncology.

items.q: A 16-year-old female presents with a suspected osteosarcoma of the proximal humerus. If an open incisional biopsy is planned, which surgical approach is recommended?
o: Through the anterior third of the deltoid
items.e: For the proximal humerus, the biopsy track must pass through the anterior third of the deltoid muscle rather than the deltopectoral groove. Dissection through the deltopectoral interval contaminates the cephalic vein, pectoralis major, and an intermuscular plane, precluding limb-sparing resection.
items.note: Classic exam question with unanimous consensus across Campbell's and sarcoma guidelines.

items.q: Which of the following is contrary to the established technical principles of an open incisional biopsy for a suspected extremity sarcoma?
o: Placing a longitudinal skin incision directly in line with the planned future resection incision
Dissecting through a muscle belly rather than entering an intermuscular or internervous plane
Creating a rounded or oval cortical window if bone fenestration is required
Exsanguinating the limb with an Esmarch compression bandage prior to tourniquet inflation
items.e: Limb exsanguination prior to tourniquet inflation should be done by limb elevation only, never by compressive wrapping with an Esmarch bandage, which carries the risk of dislodging and disseminating tumour cells into the circulation. Dissection must stay within a single compartment (through muscle, not between muscles), and bone windows should be rounded to avoid stress risers.
items.note: Clear single-best-answer testing critical biopsy technical pitfalls.

items.q: Under the AJCC 8th edition staging system for primary bone tumours of the appendicular skeleton, how is a 10 cm high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femur staged if it breaches the cortex but has no skip lesions, no nodal involvement, and no distant metastasis?
items.e: In the AJCC 8th edition for primary bone tumours, tumours measuring 8 cm or less are T1, while those larger than 8 cm are T2; discontinuous skip lesions are designated T3. A high-grade (G2/G3) lesion measuring greater than 8 cm without nodal involvement (N0) or distant metastases (M0) is classified as Stage IIB.
items.note: Tests the specific 8 cm cut-off and stage grouping of the AJCC 8th edition for bone tumours.

items.q: According to the Enneking (Musculoskeletal Tumor Society) staging system for malignant musculoskeletal lesions, which of the following is correct?
o: Lesions situated in the popliteal fossa are classified as extracompartmental by definition
Regional lymph node metastasis is categorized as stage IIB disease
A high-grade osteosarcoma confined completely within the femoral cortex is stage IIB
Intracompartmental parosteal osteosarcoma is classified as stage IIA
items.e: Anatomical regions lacking natural fascial boundaries, including the popliteal fossa, groin/femoral triangle, axilla, antecubital fossa, and intrapelvic space, are considered extracompartmental (T2) by definition. Regional lymph node involvement is considered metastatic disease (M1), assigning the lesion directly to stage III; parosteal osteosarcoma is low-grade (G1), making an intracompartmental lesion stage IA.
items.note: Accurate, distinguishing the definitions of compartments, grading, and staging under Enneking's criteria.

items.q: In the Rosen-Huvos histological grading system evaluating tumour response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in osteosarcoma, which minimum threshold of tumour necrosis defines a 'good responder'?
items.e: A histological necrosis rate of 90% or greater (Huvos Grade III [90–99%] and Grade IV [100%]) designates a 'good responder' to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Chemotherapeutic necrosis of 90% or greater serves as the single strongest prognostic indicator for overall survival in non-metastatic osteosarcoma.
items.note: Standard high-yield oncologic metric universally tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: Although the majority of extremity soft-tissue sarcomas metastasise almost exclusively via haematogenous routes to the lungs, regional lymph node staging is specifically indicated for which of the following?
items.e: Sarcomas with an established propensity for lymphatic dissemination are remembered by the mnemonic SCARE: Synovial sarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, and Epithelioid sarcoma. These histologic subtypes warrant careful regional lymph node evaluation via ultrasonography, CT, or sentinel node biopsy.
items.note: Tests the standard SCARE mnemonic for sarcomas with nodal tropism.

items.q: The FNCLCC (French Federation of Cancer Centers) histological grading system for soft-tissue sarcomas derives its prognostic score from which three parameters?
o: Tumour size, mitotic count, and vascular invasion
Tumour differentiation, mitotic count, and tumour necrosis
Cellular pleomorphism, surgical margin status, and tumour necrosis
Depth to investing fascia, tumour differentiation, and mitotic count
items.e: The FNCLCC system calculates histological grade by summing scores assigned to tumour differentiation (1–3), mitotic activity (1–3: 0–9, 10–19, >=20 per 10 HPFs), and tumour necrosis (0: none, 1: <50%, 2: >=50%). A combined score of 2–3 corresponds to Grade 1, 4–5 to Grade 2, and 6–8 to Grade 3.
items.note: Tests the exact component criteria of the most widely accepted soft-tissue sarcoma grading system.

items.q: A 38-year-old man who underwent intramedullary nailing for a closed tibial fracture 8 months ago presents with persistent localized calf pain and low-grade fever. Radiographs show delayed union and periosteal reaction. Deep tissue specimens are harvested intraoperatively. According to the international consensus definition of fracture-related infection (FRI; Metsemakers et al., updated by Govaert et al.), which of the following findings alone confirms the diagnosis of FRI?
o: Isolation of Staphylococcus epidermidis in a single deep tissue culture specimen
Persistent serosanguinous wound drainage documented for 10 days postoperatively
Histopathological finding of more than 5 neutrophils per high-power field in deep tissue specimens
Radiological evidence of focal periosteal reaction and progressive peri-implant lysis
items.e: Under the international FRI consensus criteria, confirmatory features include a sinus or wound breakdown communicating with the bone/implant, pus, phenotypically indistinguishable organisms in at least two separate deep cultures, or histopathology demonstrating microorganisms or >5 neutrophils per high-power field. A pathogen in only a single sample, persistent wound drainage, and radiological lysis are classified as suggestive criteria.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question testing the updated international FRI consensus definition.

items.q: A 56-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic venous stasis presents with chronic tibial osteomyelitis. Radiographs and CT show full-thickness cortical sequestration across a 5-cm segment of the diaphysis. Surgical excision of the necrotic segment results in a complete circumferential structural gap, producing mechanical instability. Under the Cierny-Mader staging system, this clinical scenario is classified as:
items.e: In the Cierny-Mader classification, anatomical Type IV (diffuse) involves through-and-through infection creating mechanical instability before or after debridement. The host status is compromised both systemically (diabetes = Bs) and locally (chronic venous stasis = Bl), designating the patient as a combined compromised host (Bls).
items.note: Strictly tests standard Cierny-Mader staging rules with clear-cut clinical descriptors.

items.q: A 62-year-old man presents with acute right knee septic arthritis. During arthroscopy, the surgeon notes marked synovial thickening with dense fibrin deposition forming intra-articular septations and multiple 'sponge-like' compartments. The underlying articular cartilage is preserved without subchondral osteolysis. According to Gächter's arthroscopic staging of septic arthritis, which stage is this and what is the definitive surgical recommendation?
o: Stage II; arthroscopic lavage and suction drainage
Stage III; arthroscopic synovectomy and debridement
Stage III; conversion to open arthrotomy and debridement
Stage IV; open arthrotomy with radical synovectomy
items.e: Gächter Stage III is characterized by thickened synovium with compartment formation ('sponge-like' appearance) and is treated with arthroscopic synovectomy and debridement (often requiring repeat procedures). Stage IV involves aggressive pannus infiltrating and undermining cartilage with subchondral osteolysis, necessitating open arthrotomy.
items.note: Accurately assesses the widely examined Gächter staging system and its surgical implications.

items.q: Regarding the biological characteristics and timeline of the Masquelet induced-membrane technique for reconstructing large post-infectious segmental diaphyseal defects, which of the following statements is correct?
o: The PMMA cement spacer induces a vascular membrane secreting VEGF, TGF-beta, and BMP-2; stage 2 cancellous autografting is performed at 4 to 8 weeks
The induced membrane is an avascular fibrous barrier that must be completely excised at 2 weeks prior to structural autograft placement
Stage 2 cancellous autograft packing should be delayed until 16 to 24 weeks to ensure complete collagenous maturation of the sheath
The biological sheath induces cortical bone resorption via osteoclast-activating factor and requires an immediate vascularised fibular transfer
items.e: The Masquelet technique utilizes a temporary PMMA spacer that induces a highly vascular biological envelope secreting osteogenic and angiogenic factors including VEGF, TGF-beta, and BMP-2. At stage 2 (typically at 4 to 8 weeks), the membrane is carefully incised, the spacer removed, and the interior cavity packed with cancellous autograft.
items.note: Tests critical surgical and biological principles of the Masquelet technique without ambiguity.

items.q: A 34-year-old home aquarium hobbyist presents with an indolent, progressive nodular swelling and tenosynovitis over the flexor aspect of his right index finger after cleaning a fish tank. Tissue biopsy reveals chronic necrotising granulomatous inflammation. Which pathogen is most characteristic of this presentation, and what is its distinctive culture requirement?
o: Pasteurella multocida; enriched sheep blood agar at 42°C
Sporothrix schenckii; strictly anaerobic culture at 25°C
items.e: Mycobacterium marinum causes granulomatous tenosynovitis ('fish tank granuloma') following aquatic or aquarium-related puncture wounds. It grows optimally at cooler temperatures (30°C to 32°C) and may fail to isolate if cultures are incubated solely at the standard 37°C.
items.note: Classic presentation and high-yield microbiological detail frequently tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 22-year-old athlete presents with aching pain in the proximal tibia. Plain radiography demonstrates a circumscribed metaphyseal radiolucency with a sclerotic rim. T1-weighted MRI demonstrates the 'penumbra sign', confirming subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess) rather than a bone neoplasm. The penumbra sign on non-contrast T1-weighted images corresponds to:
o: A peripheral ring of vascularized granulation tissue lining the abscess cavity
Hyperdense sclerotic cortical bone encasing an avascular central sequestrum
Extracellular methemoglobin accumulation within an intraosseous hematoma
Surrounding reactive subperiosteal fat necrosis and marrow edema
items.e: The penumbra sign on MRI consists of a discrete rim of slightly higher T1 signal lining an abscess cavity, corresponding histopathologically to vascularized granulation tissue. It is characteristic of subacute osteomyelitis/Brodie abscess and helps distinguish it from malignant bone tumors.
items.note: Tests an important radiological-pathological sign commonly tested in musculoskeletal infection.

items.q: Recent landmark trials have evaluated the duration and delivery of antimicrobial therapy in osteoarticular infections. Which of the following trial results accurately reflects current evidence?
o: In the OVIVA trial (Li et al., 2019), intravenous therapy showed significant clinical superiority over oral switch therapy in preventing treatment failure at 1 year
In native-joint septic arthritis in adults treated with surgical drainage, 2 weeks of antibiotic therapy was non-inferior to 4 weeks (Gjika et al., 2019)
In native vertebral osteomyelitis, 12 weeks of antimicrobial therapy was significantly superior to 6 weeks in achieving cure (Bernard et al., 2015)
In fracture-related infection with implant retention, 2 weeks of oral fluoroquinolone monotherapy is non-inferior to 12 weeks of combination therapy
items.e: Gjika et al. (Ann Rheum Dis 2019) demonstrated that 2 weeks of targeted antibiotic therapy following surgical drainage for native-joint septic arthritis is non-inferior to 4 weeks. In the OVIVA trial, oral antibiotics were non-inferior to IV therapy during the first 6 weeks, and Bernard et al. (Lancet 2015) established that 6 weeks of antibiotics is as effective as 12 weeks for vertebral osteomyelitis.
items.note: Tests recent landmark clinical trials that have reshaped orthopaedic infection guidelines.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presents with acute, excruciating left knee pain, tense effusion, and inability to bear weight. Arthrocentesis yields turbid fluid containing 78,000 leukocytes/mm³ with 91% neutrophils. Polarised light microscopy identifies intracellular, needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals. What is the most appropriate management strategy?
o: Initiate high-dose systemic colchicine alone, as crystal identification excludes septic arthritis
Inject intra-articular corticosteroids immediately to treat the acute rheumatoid-gout flare
Proceed with urgent joint drainage and start empirical antibiotics while awaiting cultures, as sepsis can coexist with crystal arthropathy
Defer surgical drainage and antibiotics until microbial growth is confirmed by 48-hour synovial fluid cultures
items.e: Identification of crystals (gout or pseudogout) does not exclude concurrent bacterial septic arthritis, which can trigger or coexist with crystal shedding. Given a synovial WBC >50,000/mm³ with >90% polymorphonuclear cells and severe clinical signs in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis (the strongest risk factor for septic arthritis), urgent joint drainage and empirical antibiotics are mandatory.
items.note: Tests a crucial clinical pitfall and standard emergency management principle in septic arthritis.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a 2-month history of dull right groin pain and an antalgic limp. On examination, the right hip is held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation, with an apparent lengthening of 1.5 cm. Radiographs show periarticular osteopenia with preserved joint space. According to the stages of tuberculous arthritis of the hip, which stage is this patient in?
items.e: Stage I (synovitis) of hip tuberculosis is characterised by an attitude of flexion, abduction, and external rotation, producing apparent limb lengthening due to pelvic tilt, with radiographs showing osteopenia but preserved or widened joint space.
items.note: Accurate clinical staging question aligned with Tuli's classification.
items.reason: repeats fai20261120_124 (hip TB stage I attitude)

items.q: In advanced tuberculous arthritis of the knee, destruction and secondary soft-tissue contractures lead to a characteristic 'triple deformity'. This deformity comprises flexion of the knee along with which displacements of the tibia?
items.e: The triple deformity of the tuberculous knee consists of flexion, posterior subluxation, and external rotation of the tibia (often with valgus), caused by hamstring and iliotibial band contracture.
items.note: Standard exam classic; options and answer are exact.

items.q: The classic radiographic Phemister triad of tuberculous arthritis includes all of the following features EXCEPT:
o: Gradual narrowing of the joint space
items.e: Phemister triad consists of juxta-articular osteoporosis, peripheral (marginal) erosions, and gradual (slow) joint space narrowing. Cartilage is preserved until late due to the lack of abundant proteolytic enzymes in M. tuberculosis, unlike pyogenic arthritis which causes rapid joint space loss.
items.note: Standard eponym triad tested in orthopaedic exams.

items.q: When aspirating a tuberculous cold abscess under the 'middle path' regimen, which technique is specifically recommended to avoid creating a persistent chronic discharging sinus?
o: Direct perpendicular puncture over the point of maximum skin thinning
Dependent trocar puncture to permit continuous gravitational drainage
Open incision followed by corrugated rubber drain placement
Aspiration via a non-dependent, oblique track traversing healthy tissue
items.e: Cold abscesses should be aspirated through a non-dependent, oblique, tangential track through healthy skin to allow the tissue planes to collapse upon needle withdrawal, preventing persistent sinus formation and secondary pyogenic infection.
items.note: Core surgical principle in cold abscess management.

items.q: A 42-year-old manual labourer presents with chronic, dull aching pain and restricted range of motion in the right shoulder. Examination reveals severe deltoid and periscapular wasting, but no warmth, erythema, swelling, or sinus. Radiographs show marked osteopenia and erosions of the humeral head without an identifiable cold abscess. This clinical presentation is typical of:
items.e: Caries sicca is the dry, atrophic form of tuberculosis typically encountered in the shoulder of adults; it presents with marked wasting, painful stiffness, and bony erosions without cold abscess or sinus formation.
items.note: Classic eponym and site-specific presentation.

items.q: According to the updated 2021 WHO definition, extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is defined as multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) with additional resistance to:
o: A fluoroquinolone and at least one of bedaquiline or linezolid
A fluoroquinolone and any second-line injectable agent
items.e: Under the 2021 WHO definition, XDR-TB is defined as MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one Group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid).
items.note: High-yield updated WHO definition.

items.q: A 35-year-old aquarium enthusiast develops indolent flexor tenosynovitis of the right index finger following a minor scratch sustained while cleaning a tropical fish tank. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. At which temperature should specimens be incubated to optimize culture recovery of the suspected causative mycobacterium?
items.e: Mycobacterium marinum classically causes cutaneous granulomas and tenosynovitis after marine or fish tank exposure; it has an optimal growth temperature of 30–32 °C rather than the standard 37 °C.
items.note: Precise microbiological detail frequently tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A patient being treated with first-line antitubercular therapy for knee tuberculosis reports progressive difficulty discriminating red and green colours and worsening visual acuity. Which drug is responsible for this adverse effect?
items.e: Ethambutol can cause retrobulbar optic neuritis, classically manifesting as decreased visual acuity and impaired red-green colour perception.
items.note: Direct, classic pharmacology question in osteoarticular TB.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with progressive lower limb bowing and disproportionate short stature. Clinical examination reveals widened wrists and genu varum, but muscle tone and proximal muscle strength are normal, and there is no history of tetany or seizures. Biochemical testing shows normal serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and normal serum PTH. Which gene defect is most likely responsible?
items.e: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH) is caused by inactivating mutations in the PHEX gene. Unlike calcipenic rickets, XLH typically features normal serum calcium and PTH levels, low serum phosphate due to renal phosphate wasting, and a distinct absence of proximal myopathy and tetany.
items.note: Accurate presentation, biochemistry, and genetics of XLH.

items.q: In adult osteomalacia, Looser zones (pseudofractures) are characteristically found on which of the following cortical sites?
o: Medial cortex of the femoral neck
Lateral cortex of the subtrochanteric femur
Convex cortex of the bowed tibial diaphysis
Superior border of the scapular spine
items.e: Looser zones represent unmineralised osteoid seams that occur characteristically on the concave (compression) side of bones, such as the medial femoral neck, pubic and ischial rami, and the lateral/axillary border of the scapula. In contrast, atypical femoral fractures and Paget disease pseudofractures classically involve the lateral or convex cortex.
items.note: Classic orthopaedic and metabolic bone disease question with unambiguous distractor differentiation.

items.q: Endochondral ossification failure in rickets is primarily localized to which specific histological zone of the physis?
items.e: Low phosphate impairs the programmed apoptosis of late hypertrophic chondrocytes, causing the hypertrophic zone to widen significantly while the zone of provisional calcification fails to mineralise. This gives rise to the classic rachitic physis widening, cupping, and flaring.
items.note: High-yield basic science knowledge confirmed across standard texts.

items.q: Transiliac bone biopsy with double tetracycline labelling is the gold standard for confirming osteomalacia. Which histomorphometric finding establishes the diagnosis?
o: Osteoid seam thickness under 5 µm with mineralisation lag time over 100 days
Decreased unmineralised osteoid volume with mineralisation lag time under 30 days
Woven bone predominance with scalloped resorption pits
Osteoid seam thickness over 15 µm with mineralisation lag time over 100 days
items.e: The histomorphometric hallmark of osteomalacia is defective bone mineralisation defined by an increased osteoid seam thickness (greater than 15 µm) combined with a prolonged mineralisation lag time (greater than 100 days).
items.note: Exact histomorphometric criteria matching standard metabolic bone pathology references.

items.q: A 5-year-old child with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets shows persistent skeletal deformities and growth delay despite standard oral phosphate and calcitriol therapy. Which targeted biologic agent has demonstrated superior healing of rickets and improved growth velocity in paediatric clinical trials?
items.e: Burosumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody against FGF23 administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks in children. In paediatric phase 3 trials, it significantly outperformed conventional therapy (oral phosphate and active vitamin D) in reducing rickets severity, restoring serum phosphate, and improving linear growth.
items.note: Directly tests recent evidence-based management of XLH.

items.q: What is the earliest radiographic sign indicating successful response to medical therapy in a child with nutritional rickets?
o: Complete spontaneous remodeling of diaphyseal bowing
Resolution of metaphyseal cupping and flaring
Reappearance of a dense line of provisional calcification
Restoration of normal cortical thickness across diaphyses
items.e: The earliest radiographic evidence of healing is the reappearance of a dense, transverse line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis, usually evident within 2 to 4 weeks of starting treatment. Resolution of metaphyseal flaring and diaphyseal remodelling are late phenomena occurring over months to years.
items.note: Fixed option B from a biochemical parameter ('Normalization of serum alkaline phosphatase') to a purely radiographic distractor to maintain option homogeneity.

items.q: According to the 2016 Global Consensus on nutritional rickets, which serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] threshold defines vitamin D deficiency?
items.e: The 2016 Global Consensus classifies vitamin D status based on serum 25(OH)D as: deficient at less than 30 nmol/L (<12 ng/mL), insufficient between 30 and 50 nmol/L (12-20 ng/mL), and sufficient at greater than 50 nmol/L (>20 ng/mL).
items.note: Direct reference to the definitive 2016 Global Consensus criteria.

items.q: An 8-year-old child with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets is scheduled for elective lower limb corrective osteotomy requiring postoperative cast immobilization. Which perioperative management step is essential to prevent acute complications?
o: Increase calcitriol dosage to accelerate osteotomy healing
Continue high-dose intravenous calcium infusions throughout the bed-rest period
Administer prophylactic pamidronate to prevent disuse osteopenia
Stop calcitriol a few days before prolonged immobilization
items.e: Calcitriol promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention; during periods of prolonged immobilisation or cast placement, continued administration carries a high risk of acute hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria. Calcitriol should be held a few days prior to immobilisation and resumed once full weight-bearing and mobilisation begin.
items.note: Standard perioperative endocrine rule in paediatric orthopaedic management of rickets.

items.q: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman treated with denosumab (60 mg SC 6-monthly) for 4 years stops her injections without medical advice and misses her next two scheduled doses. Seven months after her last missed dose, she presents with severe back pain and is diagnosed with multiple new spontaneous vertebral fractures. Which underlying pathophysiological mechanism accounts for this clinical presentation?
o: Accumulation of unmineralised osteoid leading to acute osteomalacia
Rebound surge in bone turnover and rapid loss of bone mineral density
Irreversible inhibition of farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteocytes
Severe inhibition of Wnt signalling by elevated circulating sclerostin
items.e: Discontinuing or delaying denosumab beyond approximately 7 months leads to a rebound surge in bone turnover, rapid loss of BMD, and a high risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures. Denosumab does not permanently bind bone, so stopping it without switching to a bisphosphonate causes rapid reversal of its antiresorptive effect.
items.note: Accurate, exam-worthy question testing a critical denosumab withdrawal clinical concept.

items.q: In the landmark HORIZON-RFT trial evaluating zoledronic acid (5 mg IV yearly) administered after surgical repair of a low-trauma hip fracture, which significant clinical outcome was uniquely demonstrated in the treatment group compared to placebo?
o: Complete prevention of atypical femoral fractures
Significant reduction in all-cause mortality by approximately 28%
Accelerated cortical fracture union at 6 weeks postoperatively
Superiority over teriparatide in spine BMD accretion at 1 year
items.e: The HORIZON-RFT trial demonstrated that a yearly 5 mg IV zoledronate infusion started after hip fracture surgery reduced new clinical fractures by 35% and reduced overall all-cause mortality by approximately 28%.
items.note: High-yield trial evidence directly relevant to orthopaedic practice and entrance examinations.

items.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as alendronate, risedronate, and zoledronate reduce osteoclastic bone resorption predominantly by inhibiting which enzyme?
o: Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway within osteoclasts. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases, leading to loss of the ruffled border and osteoclast apoptosis.
items.note: Classic pharmacology question frequently tested in orthopaedic postgraduate entrance exams.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman on continuous alendronate therapy for 7 years sustains a low-energy, complete, non-comminuted transverse subtrochanteric fracture with lateral cortical beaking. Radiographs of the contralateral asymptomatic femur demonstrate a visible focal transverse fracture line along the thickened lateral cortex in the subtrochanteric region, and on direct questioning, she reports mild prodromal thigh aching. What is the most appropriate definitive management for the contralateral femur?
o: Reassurance, bed rest, and annual DXA monitoring
Open reduction and lateral non-locking plate fixation
High-dose oral calcitonin and full weight-bearing as tolerated
items.e: For an incomplete atypical femoral fracture (AFF) with a visible fracture line (dreaded black line) or prodromal pain, prophylactic intramedullary nailing is indicated along with stopping the bisphosphonate. Plate fixation is associated with higher failure rates in AFFs.
items.note: Crucial clinical scenario matching standard ASBMR task force guidelines and orthopaedic management.

items.q: Intermittent subcutaneous administration of teriparatide (recombinant PTH 1-34) is an effective osteoanabolic agent for severe osteoporosis. However, it is CONTRAINDICATED in all of the following patients EXCEPT:
o: A 62-year-old woman with severe glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis
A 65-year-old man with Paget disease of bone and an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase
A 58-year-old woman with a prior history of radiation therapy to the skeleton
items.e: Teriparatide is indicated and effective in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (proven superior to alendronate in reducing vertebral fractures). It is contraindicated in Paget disease, unexplained raised ALP, open epiphyses, prior skeletal radiation, and skeletal malignancies due to increased risk of osteosarcoma.
items.note: Clear, unambiguous question testing absolute contraindications versus approved indications of teriparatide.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis (T-score -3.2, recent vertebral fracture) is evaluated for osteoanabolic therapy. Her medical history reveals that she suffered an acute myocardial infarction 8 months ago. Which of the following agents is explicitly CONTRAINDICATED in this patient due to cardiovascular safety signals identified in trial data?
items.e: In the ARCH trial, romosozumab (anti-sclerostin antibody) demonstrated superior fracture reduction compared to alendronate, but showed an imbalance in serious cardiovascular events (MI and stroke). It is contraindicated in patients with a myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding 12 months.
items.note: High-yield modern pharmacology topic testing black box safety warnings and trial findings.

items.q: Based on findings from the DATA-Switch study, what occurs when a postmenopausal osteoporotic patient is transitioned directly from denosumab to teriparatide monotherapy?
o: A synergistic, rapid increase in hip BMD superior to combination therapy
Progressive or transient loss of BMD, particularly at the hip
Immediate stabilization of hip BMD without any change in bone remodelling markers
Complete prevention of osteoclastic activity for up to 2 years
items.e: The DATA-Switch study demonstrated that transitioning directly from denosumab to teriparatide monotherapy causes transient or progressive loss of bone mineral density, especially at the hip, because teriparatide fails to block the rebound bone resorption triggered by denosumab withdrawal.
items.note: Tests critical sequencing knowledge regarding osteoanabolic and antiresorptive agents.

items.q: According to current guidelines (such as the ASBMR task force), which of the following postmenopausal patients is the most suitable candidate for initiating a 2 to 3 year 'bisphosphonate drug holiday'?
o: A patient who completed 3 years of annual IV zoledronate, has a current total hip T-score of -2.1, and has experienced no incident fractures
A patient who completed 5 years of oral alendronate and has a current femoral neck T-score of -2.8
A patient who completed 3 years of oral alendronate and sustained a new clinical vertebral fracture while on treatment
A patient who completed 5 years of denosumab 60 mg 6-monthly with a current hip T-score of -2.0
items.e: A bisphosphonate drug holiday (2-3 years) can be considered after 3 years of IV zoledronate or 5 years of oral bisphosphonates in patients who are not at high risk (no recent fractures and hip T-score above -2.5). High-risk patients (T-score -2.5 or below, prior hip/vertebral fracture) should continue treatment up to 6 years IV or 10 years oral. Drug holidays do not apply to denosumab.
items.note: Tests well-established ASBMR guidelines on drug holidays and patient risk stratification.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with acute monoarthritis of the knee. Synovial fluid analysis with compensated polarised light microscopy demonstrates strongly negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals that appear yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis. Which crystal is responsible for this condition?
items.e: Monosodium urate crystals causing gout are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent, appearing yellow when parallel to the compensator axis and blue when perpendicular.
items.note: Accurate, standard board-level question directly tested in entrance exams.

items.q: A 56-year-old man is diagnosed with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD). Radiographs of his hands show marked degenerative changes with hook-like osteophytes at the radial aspect of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. Which underlying metabolic disorder should be specifically suspected?
items.e: Haemochromatosis is one of the classic metabolic associations of CPPD (the '4 H's') and characteristically causes hook-like osteophytes at the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints.
items.note: High-yield classic clinical pearl in metabolic crystal arthropathies.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute, excruciating right shoulder pain. Radiographs reveal a translucent, ill-defined, fluffy calcific deposit near the supraspinatus insertion, classified as Gartner type III. In which stage of Uhthoff's reactive calcification process does this acute, highly painful phase occur?
items.e: The resorptive phase of calcific tendinitis is characterised by vascular and macrophage invasion to clear toothpaste-like calcium, resulting in high intratendinous pressure and maximum pain.
items.note: Accurate classification and staging question routinely tested in orthopaedic exams.

items.q: Before initiating allopurinol for urate-lowering therapy in a patient of Han Chinese or Thai descent with chronic gout, screening for which genetic allele is recommended to prevent severe cutaneous adverse reactions?
items.e: HLA-B*5801 screening is recommended prior to starting allopurinol in high-risk ethnic groups (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai, African-American) due to a high risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome, SJS, and TEN.
items.note: Crucial guideline-backed pharmacogenomic question.

items.q: An 80-year-old woman presents with severe acute neck pain, fever, cervical stiffness, and elevated C-reactive protein. Non-contrast CT of the cervical spine demonstrates dense calcification surrounding the odontoid process within the transverse ligament. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Crowned dens syndrome is an acute CPPD manifestation involving calcification around the dens within the transverse ligament, presenting with severe neck pain, fever, and raised inflammatory markers mimicking meningitis.
items.note: Classic diagnostic scenario in geriatric orthopaedics.

items.q: According to current guidelines (ACR 2020 / EULAR) based on the AGREE trial, what is the recommended low-dose oral colchicine regimen for treating an acute gout flare?
o: 1.2 mg immediately, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later
0.6 mg every hour until symptom resolution or diarrhoea occurs
items.e: Low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later) is as effective as high-dose regimens for acute gout flares while causing significantly less diarrhoea and toxicity.
items.note: Important evidence-based therapeutic dosage question.

items.q: Which radiological feature is characteristic of chronic tophaceous gout, helping to distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Punched-out erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
Marginal erosions in the bare area without sclerosis
items.e: Gout classically shows punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign), with preserved joint space and absence of periarticular osteopenia until late.
items.note: Standard radiological differentiator between gout and rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: An elderly woman presents with rapid joint destruction of the right shoulder, a massive rotator cuff tear, and a large blood-stained effusion. Light microscopy shows non-birefringent crystal clumps that stain positive with alizarin red S. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Milwaukee shoulder syndrome is caused by basic calcium phosphate (BCP / hydroxyapatite) crystal deposition, presenting in elderly women with destructive shoulder arthropathy, massive cuff tears, haemorrhagic effusion, and non-birefringent crystals positive for alizarin red S.
items.note: Classic presentation and histochemical identification of BCP disease.

items.q: A 62-year-old male evaluated for severe anterolateral femoral bowing and an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase undergoes a bone biopsy. Histological examination reveals a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone with prominent irregular cement (reversal) lines. On electron microscopy, hyper-nucleated giant osteoclasts from this specimen are most likely to show which of the following characteristic ultrastructural findings?
items.e: In Paget disease of bone, hyper-nucleated giant osteoclasts (containing up to 100 nuclei) characteristically demonstrate intranuclear nucleocapsid-like inclusions on electron microscopy, which forms the basis of the paramyxovirus hypothesis.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed higher-order MCQ based on reference notes and standard pathology.

items.q: A 68-year-old male with known Paget disease of the femur sustains a displaced femoral neck fracture after a fall. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical treatment strategy for this patient?
o: Closed reduction and multiple cancellous screw fixation
Dynamic hip screw fixation with a side plate
Hip arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty)
items.e: Femoral neck fractures in pagetic bone have a high non-union rate when managed with internal fixation; therefore, joint replacement (arthroplasty) is the preferred procedure.
items.note: High-yield standard orthopaedic board question directly supported by Campbell and reference notes.

items.q: A 54-year-old woman with persistent hypercalcaemia and elevated intact PTH undergoes radiological evaluation. Which of the following radiographic features is considered pathognomonic for hyperparathyroidism?
o: Subperiosteal bone resorption on the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the second and third fingers
Thickened iliopectineal line on the pelvis ('brim sign')
Dense sclerotic endplate bands with a lucent central body ('rugger-jersey spine')
Sclerotic ring around a radiolucent epiphysis ('Wimberger ring sign')
items.e: Subperiosteal resorption along the radial side of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers is a pathognomonic radiological sign of hyperparathyroidism.
items.note: Classic diagnostic radiological sign in metabolic bone disease, completely accurate.

items.q: A 42-year-old adult presents with low-energy metatarsal stress fractures, a history of premature loss of deciduous teeth with intact roots, low total serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and raised serum pyridoxal-5-phosphate. Which of the following medical therapies is strictly contraindicated in this condition?
items.e: In hypophosphatasia (caused by ALPL gene mutations resulting in low serum ALP), bisphosphonates are contraindicated because they are pyrophosphate analogues that further impair bone mineralisation.
items.note: Important clinical contraindication topic for entrance exams, accurately formulated.

items.q: A 3-year-old child fed on an exclusive unfortified boiled-milk diet presents with painful pseudoparalysis of the lower limbs, perifollicular skin haemorrhages, and tender metaphyseal swellings around the knees. Knee radiographs show a dense zone of provisional calcification at the metaphysis. What is the name of this classic sign?
items.e: The White line of Frankel is the dense zone of provisional calcification seen at the metaphysis in scurvy; the radiolucent zone immediately beneath it is the Trummerfeld zone.
items.note: Classic pediatric metabolic bone disease sign, distractor choices are well-matched scurvy signs.

items.q: A 50-year-old agricultural worker from an endemic region presents with progressive spinal rigidity, joint pain, and bilateral forearm stiffness. Plain radiographs demonstrate diffuse osteosclerosis of the spine, pelvis, and ribs, alongside prominent calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane and sacrotuberous ligaments. What is the key mechanism driving this condition?
o: Replacement of hydroxyl groups in hydroxyapatite by fluoride to form fluorapatite
Defective hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen synthesis
items.e: In skeletal fluorosis, fluoride replaces hydroxyl groups in hydroxyapatite to form dense but brittle fluorapatite bone, leading to widespread osteosclerosis and ligamentous/interosseous membrane calcification.
items.note: High relevance in Indian exams; scientifically accurate and robust.

items.q: A 58-year-old patient on maintenance haemodialysis for 14 years presents with bilateral severe carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical destructive spondyloarthropathy, and subchondral bone cysts in the hips. Which protein accumulation is directly responsible for this patient's presentation?
items.e: Long-term haemodialysis leads to dialysis-related amyloidosis from beta-2 microglobulin accumulation, which deposits in musculoskeletal tissues causing bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, destructive spondyloarthropathy, and subchondral bone cysts.
items.note: Standard renal osteodystrophy / dialysis complication question, accurate.

items.q: In accordance with international guidelines (Ralston et al. 2019) and the results of the PRISM trial, which of the following is the primary evidence-based indication for initiating bisphosphonate therapy in Paget disease of bone?
o: Prophylactic prevention of hearing loss in asymptomatic cranial lesions
Bone pain directly attributable to active Paget disease
Asymptomatic elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase to double the normal limit
Routine disease suppression before elective surgery on unaffected normal bones
items.e: The PRISM trial demonstrated that intensive treatment to normalize serum ALP in asymptomatic Paget disease provided no clinical advantage; bone pain attributable to active disease remains the main evidence-based indication for bisphosphonate therapy.
items.note: Reflects modern clinical guidelines and landmark trials as per reference notes.

items.q: A surgeon performing a surgical dislocation of the hip (Ganz approach) preserves the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery. Anatomically, this vessel runs between which two structures?
o: Anterior to obturator externus and posterior to piriformis
Posterior to obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators
Superior to piriformis and inferior to gluteus minimus
Posterior to the short external rotators and anterior to quadratus femoris
items.e: The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) passes posterior to the obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators (gemelli and obturator internus). Preserving this relationship is the basis of the Ganz surgical dislocation technique.
items.note: Accurate, clear anatomical fact from Campbell's directly tested in competitive SS exams.

items.q: According to the ARCO 2019 criteria, which threshold definition establishes corticosteroid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Cumulative intake of over 1 g prednisolone within 1 month, diagnosed within 5 years
Continuous daily administration of 10 mg prednisolone for 12 months, diagnosed within 6 months
Cumulative intake of over 2 g prednisolone (or equivalent) within a 3-month period, diagnosed within 2 years
Inhaled steroid therapy for over 6 months, diagnosed within 1 year
items.e: Under the ARCO 2019 criteria, glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis requires exposure to over 2 g prednisolone (or equivalent) within a 3-month period, with diagnosis made within 2 years of corticosteroid use.
items.note: Exact criteria from ARCO 2019 consensus guidelines.

items.q: A 38-year-old male with early osteonecrosis of the femoral head undergoes MRI. On T2-weighted images, a pathognomonic 'double-line sign' is visualized. What histological tissues correspond to the inner and outer lines of this sign?
o: Inner line: Sclerotic bone; Outer line: Hyperaemic granulation tissue
Inner line: Hyperaemic granulation tissue; Outer line: Sclerotic bone
Inner line: Dense fibrous tissue; Outer line: Normal fat marrow
Inner line: Subchondral fluid effusion; Outer line: Hyaline cartilage
items.e: On T2-weighted MRI, the pathognomonic double-line sign consists of an inner high-signal line representing hyperaemic granulation tissue and an outer low-signal line representing sclerotic bone.
items.note: Classic MRI feature tested repeatedly in NEET-SS/INI-SS.

items.q: During core decompression for pre-collapse osteonecrosis of the femoral head, initiating the drill entry on the lateral cortex below which level creates a significant stress riser that predisposes to subtrochanteric fracture?
items.e: Drill entry on the lateral cortex below the level of the lesser trochanter creates a stress riser and is the primary cause of post-operative subtrochanteric fractures during core decompression.
items.note: Crucial technical pearl regarding core decompression complications.

items.q: A woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with left hip pain. MRI displays diffuse bone marrow oedema involving the femoral head, neck, and extending to the intertrochanteric region, without a focal subchondral band or double-line sign. What is the standard initial management?
items.e: This clinical and MRI picture describes transient osteoporosis of the hip, which typically occurs in third-trimester pregnancy and is self-limiting over 6 to 12 months. Treatment is non-operative with protected weight bearing to prevent femoral neck fracture and analgesia.
items.note: High-yield differential diagnosis for AVN.

items.q: Using the modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle measured on coronal and sagittal MRI views, which sum indicates a high risk of femoral head collapse?
items.e: The modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle sums the arc of necrosis on mid-coronal and mid-sagittal MRI images. Angles under 190 degrees carry a low collapse risk, 190-240 degrees intermediate risk, and 240 degrees or more a high risk of collapse.
items.note: Standard prognostic classification system.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon reviews a 7-week post-injury radiograph of a talar neck fracture and identifies a subchondral radiolucent line (Hawkins sign) beneath the talar dome. What does this finding indicate?
o: Complete osteonecrosis of the talar body
Septic osteolysis due to deep infection
items.e: The Hawkins sign is subchondral radiolucency of the talar dome visible at 6-8 weeks on an AP ankle radiograph. It indicates intact blood supply and active bone resorption from disuse, making avascular necrosis unlikely.
items.note: Classic exam pearl for foot and ankle trauma.

items.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe medial knee pain that wakes her at night. MRI shows a single epiphyseal lesion measuring 2.5 cm² on the weight-bearing medial femoral condyle. What is the diagnosis and initial management?
o: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK); protected weight bearing and analgesia
items.e: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK) typically affects women over 55-60 years with sudden onset medial condyle pain. Lesions smaller than 3.5 cm² (or under 40% condylar width) have a good prognosis and are managed initially with protected weight bearing and analgesia.
items.note: Important distinction between SONK and secondary AVN of the knee.

items.q: A 4-year-old child presents with delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, absent clavicles, and hypertelorism. A clinical diagnosis of cleidocranial dysplasia is made. Which key transcription factor responsible for osteoblast differentiation is mutated in this condition?
items.e: RUNX2 (also known as CBFA1) is the master transcription factor driving mesenchymal stem cell differentiation into osteoblasts. Mutations in RUNX2 cause cleidocranial dysplasia.
items.note: Accurate, well-structured single-best-answer question directly testing key osteoblast transcription factor genetics.

items.q: During reamed intramedullary nailing of a femoral shaft fracture, the high-pressure nutrient endosteal blood supply is acutely disrupted. How does the vascular flow pattern in the cortex change immediately following this disruption?
o: Flow remains centrifugal (inside-out) via collateral channels
Flow becomes centripetal (outside-in) dominated by periosteal vessels
Flow ceases completely across all cortical layers
Flow reverses from periosteal to endosteal under elevated pressure
items.e: Normal mature bone blood flow is centrifugal (inside-out from high-pressure endosteal nutrient vessels). When the endosteal supply is disrupted by reaming or fracture displacement, flow becomes centripetal (outside-in), relying on low-pressure periosteal vessels.
items.note: Standard orthopaedic basic science question assessing vascular physiological adaptation to fracture and reaming.

items.q: A 10-year-old child suffers a Salter-Harris type II fracture of the distal radius. Through which specific physeal zone does the fracture line predominantly pass?
o: Zone of provisional calcification of the hypertrophic zone
items.e: Physeal fractures typically propagate through the weakest region of the growth plate, which is the zone of provisional calcification within the hypertrophic zone. The germinal and proliferative zones stay attached to the epiphysis.
items.note: Classic physeal anatomy question with unambiguous options directly aligned with standard orthopaedic texts.

items.q: Which pair of bone turnover markers is recommended by the International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF) and IFCC as standard reference markers for clinical and trial settings?
items.e: The IOF and IFCC recommend serum P1NP (procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide) as the standard bone formation marker and serum CTX (C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen) as the standard bone resorption marker.
items.note: High-yield guideline-based turnover marker question relevant for superspeciality orthopaedic exams.

items.q: A 65-year-old female receives an intravenous infusion of zoledronic acid for postmenopausal osteoporosis. What is the primary molecular target inhibited by nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates within osteoclasts?
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (such as zoledronate, alendronate, and risedronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases required for ruffled border formation and osteoclast function, leading to osteoclast apoptosis.
items.note: Direct, accurate question testing the core pharmacological mechanism of action of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates.

items.q: A pediatric patient evaluated for dense, fragile bones and short stature is diagnosed with Pyknodysostosis. Mutation of which lysosomal cysteine protease responsible for organic matrix breakdown causes this disease?
items.e: Pyknodysostosis is caused by a genetic defect in Cathepsin K, a lysosomal cysteine protease secreted at the osteoclast ruffled border to digest organic collagen matrix.
items.note: Clear single-best-answer question connecting bone cell enzymology to clinical pathology.

items.q: In the Masquelet induced-membrane technique for treating large segmental bone defects, a PMMA cement spacer is inserted in the first stage. At what time point after placement does the induced membrane reach its peak biological activity for key growth factor secretion?
items.e: The biological membrane induced by the PMMA spacer reaches its peak bioactivity for secreting growth factors (such as VEGF, TGF-beta, and BMP-2) at 4 to 8 weeks, making this the optimal window for second-stage spacer removal and bone grafting.
items.note: Applied operative basic science question with precise timeframe supported by orthopaedic literature.

items.q: Which non-collagenous protein is the most abundant in the organic bone matrix, requires vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation, is produced by osteoblasts under 1,25(OH)2D stimulation, and serves as a serum marker of bone formation?
items.e: Osteocalcin (bone gla protein) is the most abundant non-collagenous protein in bone matrix. Synthesized by osteoblasts, its synthesis is stimulated by 1,25(OH)2D and requires vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation; it serves as a clinical marker of bone formation.
items.note: Factually sound bone matrix biology question with distractor items from the same protein class.

items.q: A biomechanical researcher is studying joint lubrication mechanisms under high-load, static standing conditions. Which molecule forms a monolayer on the surface of articular cartilage to provide boundary lubrication under these specific conditions?
items.e: Lubricin (encoded by PRG4 and secreted by superficial zone chondrocytes and synoviocytes) acts as the primary boundary lubricant, forming a monolayer on cartilage surfaces under conditions of high load, low speed, and static standing.
items.note: Fully accurate, high-yield basic science concept directly tested in orthopaedic superspeciality exams.

items.q: Which of the following biochemical changes correctly distinguishes the cartilage alterations seen in Osteoarthritis (OA) from those of normal physiological Ageing?
o: Water content decreases in OA, whereas it increases in Ageing
Keratan sulfate levels increase in OA, whereas they decrease in Ageing
Chondroitin-4 sulfate levels increase in OA, whereas they decrease in Ageing
Cartilage permeability decreases in OA, whereas it increases in Ageing
items.e: In Osteoarthritis, chondroitin-4 sulfate levels increase while keratan sulfate levels decrease. Conversely, in physiological ageing, chondroitin-4 sulfate decreases, keratan sulfate increases, water content decreases, and tissue permeability decreases.
items.note: Accurate and directly tests a classic, highly examined table comparing cartilage ageing versus osteoarthritis.

items.q: A 35-year-old male undergoes a histological evaluation of articular cartilage from the medial femoral condyle. In which region of normal adult articular cartilage is collagen type X uniquely located?
items.e: Type X collagen is uniquely present in the calcified cartilage zone of adult articular cartilage and hypertrophic chondrocytes of the physis, where it is associated with tissue mineralisation and anchoring cartilage to subchondral bone.
items.note: Factually precise single-best-answer question based on standard orthopaedic basic science.

items.q: Based on the SUMMIT trial (Saris et al., 2014), matrix-applied autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI) was demonstrated to be superior to microfracture at 2 years in terms of pain and function for knee cartilage defects meeting which size threshold?
items.e: The SUMMIT trial (Saris et al., 2014) demonstrated that MACI was clinically and statistically superior to microfracture at 2 years for symptomatic knee articular cartilage defects measuring 3 cm² or larger.
items.note: Accurate landmark clinical trial question standard for high-level orthopaedic entrance exams.

items.q: Synoviocytes are broadly classified into Type A and Type B cells. Which of the following characteristics is true regarding Type A synoviocytes?
o: They are derived from mesenchymal cells and produce hyaluronic acid
They express CD68 and are derived from bone marrow monocyte lineage
They form the primary effector cells of the rheumatoid pannus that invade cartilage
They synthesize lubricin and type I collagen to lubricate the joint
items.e: Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-like cells derived from bone marrow monocyte lineage; they express CD68, perform phagocytosis, and present antigens. Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like mesenchymal cells that produce hyaluronic acid and lubricin.
items.note: Clear and factually verified distinction between Type A and Type B synoviocytes.
