items.q: A 62-year-old man presents with acute monoarthritis of the right knee. Synovial fluid aspiration yields cloudy fluid with a WBC count of 35,000/mm³ with 70% neutrophils. Polarized light microscopy reveals weakly positive birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals. What is the composition of these crystals?
items.e: Rhomboid- or rod-shaped crystals exhibiting weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy are characteristic of Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate (CPPD) crystals, seen in pseudogout.
items.note: Classic diagnostic scenario standard across orthopaedic SS exams.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent atraumatic bloody effusions of the left knee. MRI demonstrates a diffusely thickened synovium with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, along with prominent blooming artifact on gradient-echo sequences. What genetic alteration is characteristic of this neoplasm?
items.e: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour / pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS) is a benign neoplasm characterized by a translocation involving the CSF1 gene, causing CSF1 overexpression. MRI characteristically shows blooming on gradient-echo images due to haemosiderin.
items.note: High-yield pathology and imaging integration with distinct genetic correlation.

items.q: In the enzymatic degradation of articular cartilage in osteoarthritis, which matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) plays the predominant role in specifically cleaving native type II collagen?
items.e: MMP-13 (collagenase-3) is the primary matrix metalloproteinase responsible for degrading type II collagen in articular cartilage, whereas ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5 act predominantly as aggrecanases.
items.note: Direct, unambiguous basic science question on cartilage catabolism.

items.q: A 65-year-old male with left hip osteoarthritis is recommended conservative management including the use of a walking stick. To achieve the maximum reduction in left hip joint reaction force, in which hand should he hold the cane, and by approximately what percentage can this reduce the joint reaction force during single-leg stance?
items.e: Holding a cane in the contralateral hand provides a long lever arm relative to the hip, which dramatically reduces the required abductor muscle force and decreases the hip joint reaction force by up to 40–60% in single-leg stance.
items.note: Accurate, clinically relevant biomechanics question supported by standard references and notes.

items.q: During total joint arthroplasty, polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement is mixed on the back table. Which of the following liquid component additives acts specifically as a stabilizer/inhibitor to prevent premature polymerization during storage?
items.e: In PMMA bone cement, hydroquinone is added to the liquid monomer as an inhibitor/stabilizer to prevent premature polymerization. Benzoyl peroxide is the initiator in the powder, N,N-dimethyl-p-toluidine (DMPT) is the accelerator in the liquid, and barium sulfate is a radiopacifier in the powder.
items.note: High-yield, unambiguous basic sciences question directly testing PMMA chemical constituents.

items.q: Which of the following options correctly lists orthopaedic implant biomaterials and bone in decreasing order of Young's modulus of elasticity (stiffness)?
o: Cobalt-chrome alloy > Alumina ceramic > Stainless steel 316L > Titanium alloy > Cortical bone
Alumina ceramic > Cobalt-chrome alloy > Stainless steel 316L > Titanium alloy > Cortical bone
Alumina ceramic > Stainless steel 316L > Cobalt-chrome alloy > Cortical bone > Titanium alloy
Cobalt-chrome alloy > Stainless steel 316L > Titanium alloy > PMMA bone cement > Cortical bone
items.e: The correct sequence of stiffness (Young's modulus of elasticity) from highest to lowest is ceramic (alumina ~350–400 GPa) > CoCr alloy (~210–230 GPa) > 316L stainless steel (~190–200 GPa) > titanium alloy (~110 GPa) > cortical bone (~15–20 GPa).
items.note: Classic and frequently tested sequence question in biomaterials; fully correct.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon is applying a monoplanar unilateral external fixator for an open tibial shaft fracture. Which of the following modifications provides the GREATEST increase in construct stiffness?
o: Moving the connecting bar further away from the bone
Decreasing the distance between pins within the same fragment
Replacing carbon fibre connecting rods with stainless steel rods of identical diameter
items.e: Increasing pin diameter is the single most effective way to increase external fixator stiffness because pin bending stiffness is proportional to the pin radius raised to the fourth power (r^4).
items.note: Standard fixator mechanics question with clear, single-best mathematically supported distractor relationship.

items.q: In an ankle fracture with syndesmotic instability, lateral displacement (shift) of the talus within the ankle mortise by 1 mm reduces the tibiotalar contact area by approximately:
items.e: As demonstrated by Ramsey and Hamilton, just 1 mm of lateral talar shift reduces tibiotalar joint contact area by approximately 42%, causing a dramatic increase in local contact stress.
items.note: Classic historical and exam numerical fact in ankle trauma biomechanics.

items.q: A 62-year-old female who underwent total hip arthroplasty presents 6 years postoperatively with groin pain and an adverse local tissue reaction (pseudotumour) on MRI. Serum metal ion analysis reveals significantly elevated Cobalt levels compared to Chromium levels. This presentation is most characteristic of which type of corrosion?
items.e: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC or trunnionosis) occurs at modular head-neck taper junctions due to fretting and crevice corrosion. It leads to preferential release of cobalt over chromium and can result in pseudotumour formation.
items.note: Exam-worthy scenario on modern arthroplasty failure mechanisms and implant corrosion.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon creates a longitudinal rectangular cortical window (open-section defect) in the femoral shaft to perform a deep sequestrectomy. Compared to a round drill hole of equal width, how does an open-section defect affect the torsional strength of the bone?
o: It causes minimal change in torsional strength compared to a round hole
It increases torsional strength by dissipating torsional stress along its long axis
It reduces torsional strength drastically, by well over half (up to 90%)
It reduces torsional strength by exactly 10%
items.e: An open-section defect (such as a longitudinal cortical window or slot) drastically reduces the torsional strength of a long bone by well over half (up to 90%), which is far more detrimental than a closed round drill hole.
items.note: Definitive biomechanical concept regarding stress risers and open vs closed section defects.

items.q: Highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) liners used in total hip arthroplasty are thermally processed after high-dose irradiation to eliminate free radicals. What is the primary mechanical disadvantage of choosing REMELTING over ANNEALING during thermal processing?
o: Leaves residual free radicals that cause severe shelf-ageing oxidation
Reduces fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength
Increases wear rate compared to non-cross-linked polyethylene
items.e: Remelting cross-linked polyethylene above its melting point eliminates all free radicals but reduces the material's fatigue strength, yield strength, and toughness. Annealing preserves mechanical properties better but leaves residual free radicals behind.
items.note: High-yield question testing post-irradiation thermal processing of polyethylene in joint replacement.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy is diagnosed with localized Ewing sarcoma of the proximal femur. Based on evidence from clinical trials such as Euro Ewing 2012 and COG AEWS0031, which of the following represents the current standard first-line chemotherapy schedule?
o: European VIDE regimen given every 3 weeks
items.e: The Euro Ewing 2012 trial and COG AEWS0031 demonstrated that interval-compressed VDC/IE (vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide, etoposide) given every 2 weeks is superior to the 3-weekly VIDE regimen in both event-free and overall survival with less toxicity, making it the global standard of care.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the current global standard of care for Ewing sarcoma chemotherapy as supported by the provided notes and recent major trials.

items.q: A 62-year-old male presenting with back pain and multiple punched-out lytic bone lesions undergoes technetium-99m bone scintigraphy, which demonstrates minimal or no increased tracer uptake ('cold' bone scan). What is the underlying cellular mechanism for this finding in multiple myeloma?
o: Downregulation of RANKL expression by neoplastic plasma cells
Plasma cell secretion of DKK1 and sclerostin, suppressing osteoblasts
Excessive unmineralized osteoid production by hyperactive osteoblasts
Direct ischaemic necrosis of the bony trabeculae without osteoclasts
items.e: Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy relies on osteoblastic bone repair activity to show hyperuptake. In multiple myeloma, tumor cells secrete DKK1 and sclerostin which suppress osteoblasts (along with increasing RANKL to activate osteoclasts), resulting in purely lytic lesions without osteoclastic repair and causing a false-negative ('cold') bone scan.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the molecular basis for the classic 'cold' bone scan in myeloma as described in the reference notes.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with deep-seated thigh pain. Radiographs reveal a permeative, moth-eaten lytic lesion in the femoral diaphysis with minimal periosteal reaction. MRI shows extensive marrow replacement with a large circumferential soft-tissue mass around an intact cortex. Core biopsy confirms diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). What is the primary definitive management strategy?
o: En bloc wide resection of the diaphyseal segment followed by endoprosthetic reconstruction
Extended intralesional curettage with phenol adjuvant and polymethylmethacrylate cementation
Systemic combination chemotherapy (R-CHOP) with or without consolidation radiotherapy
Neoadjuvant MAP chemotherapy followed by limb-salvage resection
items.e: Primary bone lymphoma (DLBCL) is managed definitively with systemic chemotherapy (R-CHOP) with or without consolidation radiotherapy. Surgery plays no role in local tumor removal and is reserved solely for prophylactic or therapeutic stabilization of pathological fractures or spinal decompression.
items.note: The question correctly distinguishes the non-surgical management of primary bone lymphoma from other bone malignancies.

items.q: A biopsy of a small round blue cell tumour from the distal femur of a 12-year-old child shows strong membranous CD99 positivity and nuclear NKX2.2 expression. Cytogenetics reveals a t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation. Which fusion transcript is formed by this specific chromosomal rearrangement?
items.e: The t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation is the hallmark genetic aberration in Ewing sarcoma (accounting for ~85-90% of cases) and results in the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion transcript.
items.note: The question tests the hallmark genetic translocation of Ewing sarcoma, which is a high-yield exam fact.

items.q: According to the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG 2014) updated diagnostic criteria, which of the following is classified as a 'SLiM' biomarker defining multiple myeloma even in the absence of classic CRAB features?
o: Involved-to-uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater
Clonal bone marrow plasma cell percentage of 30% or greater
Serum beta-2 microglobulin level greater than 5.5 mg/L
Presence of at least three osteolytic lesions on conventional skeletal radiography
items.e: The IMWG 2014 SLiM biomarkers defining myeloma independent of CRAB criteria include: Sixty percent or more clonal bone marrow plasma cells; involved-to-uninvolved serum free Light-chain ratio of 100 or greater; and MRI showing More than one focal bone lesion (>=5 mm).
items.note: The question accurately tests the modern IMWG diagnostic criteria for myeloma, which have replaced older systems in clinical practice and exams.

items.q: A 16-year-old girl undergoes wide resection of a diaphyseal Ewing sarcoma of the fibula after completing 12 weeks of induction chemotherapy. Histopathological analysis of the resected specimen reveals 15% viable tumor cells. Which statement correctly categorizes this histological response and its clinical significance?
o: Good response; predicts excellent long-term event-free survival with surgery alone
Poor response; indicates an adverse prognosis and warrants consideration of postoperative radiotherapy or high-risk consolidation regimens
Complete response; no further adjuvant systemic therapy is required
Indeterminate response; tumor necrosis percentage has no prognostic value in Ewing sarcoma
items.e: In Ewing sarcoma, a poor histological response to induction chemotherapy is defined as 10% or more viable tumor cells (<90% necrosis). Poor histological response is a major adverse prognostic factor and indicates the need for postoperative radiotherapy or intensified consolidation therapy.
items.note: The question tests the specific prognostic threshold for chemotherapy response in Ewing sarcoma, which is a critical clinical parameter.

items.q: A 2-year-old child presents with progressive bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), proptosis, fever, and a palpable retroperitoneal mass. Skeletal radiographs demonstrate symmetrical, permeative lytic lesions in the metaphyses of both femora. Which laboratory test is most specific for confirming this suspected condition?
o: Serum monoclonal M-protein spike on protein electrophoresis
Elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA)
Diffuse CD45 (leucocyte common antigen) positivity on flow cytometry
items.e: The presentation of a child under 5 with periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes'), proptosis, retroperitoneal mass, and symmetric metaphyseal lytic metastases is classic for metastatic neuroblastoma. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating elevated urinary catecholamine metabolites (VMA and HVA) and MIBG-avid lesions.
items.note: The question integrates clinical signs, age, and specific diagnostic tests for neuroblastoma, a key differential in pediatric orthopaedic oncology.

items.q: When evaluating a patient presenting with a permeative 'small round blue cell' lytic bone lesion on plain radiographs, patient age serves as the single crucial initial diagnostic clue. In a child under 5 years of age, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Age is the primary diagnostic clue for small round cell bone tumours: under 5 years, metastatic neuroblastoma, leukaemia, and LCH are most common; Ewing sarcoma peaks in the second decade (5–25 years); primary lymphoma peaks in adults aged 40–60 years; and multiple myeloma occurs almost exclusively over 40–50 years.
items.note: The question tests the fundamental 'age-based' diagnostic algorithm for small round cell tumors of bone.

items.q: Which of the following soft-tissue sarcomas is the most common histological subtype found in the extremities of adults over the age of 50 years?
items.e: Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) and liposarcoma are the two most common soft-tissue sarcomas in adults. For extremity sarcomas specifically in older adults, UPS is the most frequently quoted subtype.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the most common subtype in the specified demographic based on the provided notes and standard oncology references.

items.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painless lump in his thigh. Which clinical feature would be considered a 'red flag' warranting urgent specialist referral and imaging for a suspected sarcoma?
o: A lump that has been stable for 10 years
Recurrence of a previously excised lump
items.e: Red-flag features for soft-tissue sarcoma include a size over 5 cm, location deep to the deep fascia, increasing size, pain, or recurrence after previous excision.
items.note: The options correctly distinguish between benign characteristics and established red-flag features for sarcoma.

items.q: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with a high-grade myxoid liposarcoma of the thigh. In addition to a CT of the chest for staging, which investigation is specifically recommended for this subtype due to its unique metastatic pattern?
items.e: Myxoid liposarcoma has a propensity for extrapulmonary metastasis, particularly to the spine, retroperitoneum, and other soft tissues. Therefore, staging should include whole-spine or whole-body MRI in addition to CT chest.
items.note: This is a high-yield clinical pearl regarding the specific staging requirements for myxoid liposarcoma.

items.q: According to the biopsy principles established by Mankin et al., which statement is correct regarding the management of a suspected soft-tissue sarcoma?
o: The biopsy should be performed through a transverse incision to allow better wound healing.
The biopsy tract is considered contaminated and must be excised en bloc with the tumour.
Fine-needle aspiration is the gold standard for primary histological grading.
Samples should be taken from the necrotic centre of the tumour to ensure diagnostic yield.
items.e: Standard biopsy rules for sarcoma include using a longitudinal incision, avoiding the neurovascular bundle, and ensuring the biopsy tract is excised en bloc during definitive surgery. Core needle biopsy is preferred over FNA.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the Mankin principles which are the standard of care in orthopaedic oncology.

items.q: In the FNCLCC (French) grading system for soft-tissue sarcomas, which of the following parameters is NOT used to calculate the total histological score?
items.e: The FNCLCC system uses three parameters: tumour differentiation (score 1-3), mitotic count (score 1-3), and tumour necrosis (score 0-2). Tumour size is used for AJCC T-staging, not histological grading.
items.note: The distinction between grading (histology) and staging (size/spread) is a fundamental concept in oncology exams.

items.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a painful mass near the knee. Radiographs show a soft-tissue mass with internal calcification. Genetic testing reveals a t(X;18)(p11;q11) translocation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Synovial sarcoma typically affects young adults, often presents with pain, and shows calcification in approximately 30% of cases. The characteristic genetic marker is the t(X;18) translocation involving SS18-SSX.
items.note: The clinical presentation and genetic marker provided are classic for synovial sarcoma.

items.q: Based on the NCIC SR2 trial (O'Sullivan et al.), what is the primary advantage of choosing preoperative radiotherapy over postoperative radiotherapy for extremity soft-tissue sarcomas?
o: Significantly lower rate of acute wound complications
Lower risk of late toxicities like fibrosis and joint stiffness
Elimination of the need for surgical margins
items.e: Preoperative radiotherapy uses a lower dose and smaller field than postoperative radiotherapy, leading to lower late toxicity (fibrosis, stiffness). However, it is associated with a higher rate of acute wound complications (35% vs 17%).
items.note: The O'Sullivan trial is the landmark study cited in Campbell's and other major texts regarding radiotherapy timing.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman is diagnosed with a 5 cm asymptomatic desmoid-type fibromatosis in her shoulder girdle. According to the 2020 global consensus (Desmoid Tumor Working Group), what is the recommended first-line management?
o: Wide local excision with 2 cm margins
items.e: Modern management of desmoid fibromatosis prioritizes active surveillance as the first-line approach because these tumours are locally infiltrative but never metastasise, and many may stabilise or regress spontaneously.
items.note: This reflects the current international consensus which has shifted away from immediate aggressive surgery for desmoids.

items.q: A 58-year-old male presents with a painful lytic lesion in the distal phalanx of the index finger. A chest radiograph reveals a peripheral mass in the right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis for the digital lesion?
items.e: Acrometastases (metastases distal to the elbow and knee) are rare; however, when they occur, the commonest primary site is the lung. Breast and prostate cancers rarely spread to the hands and feet.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the clinical association between acrometastases and lung cancer as the primary source, which is a classic orthopaedic oncology fact.

items.q: In the 'vicious cycle' of osteolytic bone metastasis, which factor is directly secreted by tumour cells to stimulate osteoblasts to express RANKL?
items.e: Tumour cells secrete PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein), which stimulates osteoblasts to increase RANKL expression. This activates osteoclasts, leading to bone resorption and the release of growth factors like TGF-beta from the matrix, which further stimulates the tumour.
items.note: The pathophysiology of the 'vicious cycle' is a core concept in metastatic bone disease and is accurately represented here.

items.q: A 62-year-old male with no prior history of malignancy presents with a solitary lytic lesion of the proximal humerus. According to the Rougraff diagnostic strategy for skeletal metastasis of unknown origin, which primary is most commonly identified?
items.e: In patients presenting with a skeletal metastasis of unknown origin, the Rougraff strategy (history, exam, labs, CXR, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and bone scan) identifies the primary in 85% of cases. Lung (non-small cell) is the most common unknown primary, followed by kidney.
items.note: The question tests the specific findings of the Rougraff study, which is the standard reference for evaluating unknown primary bone lesions.

items.q: A 55-year-old woman with known breast cancer presents with a peritrochanteric lytic lesion involving 75% of the femoral cortical diameter. She experiences significant mechanical pain on weight-bearing. What is her Mirels score and the recommended management?
items.e: The Mirels score is 12 (Site: peritrochanteric = 3; Pain: functional/mechanical = 3; Lesion: lytic = 3; Size: >2/3 diameter = 3). A score of 9 or more indicates a high risk of fracture (33% or more) and warrants prophylactic fixation.
items.note: The calculation of the Mirels score is accurate based on the provided clinical variables, and the management recommendation follows standard guidelines.

items.q: A 50-year-old patient is diagnosed with a solitary, expansile 'blow-out' metastatic lesion in the humerus from a renal cell carcinoma. Which perioperative step is most critical to reduce the risk of massive intraoperative bleeding during stabilization?
o: Use of a locked intramedullary nail without reaming
items.e: Renal cell and thyroid metastases are classically hypervascular. Preoperative embolization is essential to reduce surgical blood loss and should be performed 24-72 hours before the procedure.
items.note: The question addresses a critical surgical principle for specific hypervascular metastases (renal and thyroid).

items.q: According to the results of the randomized trial by Patchell et al. (2005), which of the following is an inclusion criterion for performing direct decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy in metastatic spinal cord compression?
o: Expected survival of at least 3 months
items.e: The Patchell trial showed surgery plus radiotherapy is superior to radiotherapy alone for MSCC from solid tumours if: there is a single area of compression, paraplegia has lasted less than 48 hours, and expected survival is at least 3 months.
items.note: The Patchell trial is a landmark study in spinal oncology, and its inclusion/exclusion criteria are frequently tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: Which MRI finding is most characteristic of a malignant vertebral collapse as opposed to an osteoporotic insufficiency fracture?
o: Preservation of normal fatty marrow signal
Convex bulge of the posterior cortex
items.e: Malignant vertebral collapse is characterized by a convex bulge of the posterior cortex, diffuse T1 low signal replacing the whole marrow, and involvement of the pedicles. Vacuum clefts and preserved fatty marrow are typical of osteoporotic fractures.
items.note: The differentiation between malignant and osteoporotic vertebral collapse on MRI is a high-yield clinical skill tested in oncology modules.

items.q: Regarding bone-targeted agents in the management of skeletal metastases, which statement is correct?
o: Zoledronic acid is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL
Denosumab requires dose adjustment in patients with renal impairment
Denosumab is superior to zoledronic acid in delaying the first skeletal-related event in breast and prostate cancer
Bisphosphonates must be stopped immediately if osteonecrosis of the jaw is suspected
items.e: Denosumab (anti-RANKL antibody) has been shown to be superior to zoledronic acid in delaying the first skeletal-related event (SRE) in breast and prostate cancer. It does not require renal dose adjustment, unlike zoledronic acid.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the pharmacological differences and clinical trial outcomes (Stopeck/Fizazi) comparing bisphosphonates and denosumab.

items.q: A 19-year-old male presents with a suspicious destructive lesion in the proximal humerus. If an open biopsy is planned, which of the following surgical approaches is most appropriate to avoid contaminating multiple compartments?
o: Through the anterior third of the deltoid
Lateral approach through the deltoid-triceps interval
items.e: According to technical rules for biopsy, the incision should be longitudinal and go through a muscle (like the anterior third of the deltoid) rather than between muscles. The deltopectoral groove is avoided because an intermuscular plane contaminates two compartments (deltoid and pectoralis major) and the cephalic vein.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the preferred biopsy route for the proximal humerus as per Campbell's and the provided notes.

items.q: In the diagnostic workup of a suspected primary bone sarcoma, why must local staging with MRI be performed before a biopsy is taken?
o: To prevent the spread of tumor cells during imaging
Because biopsy-induced hematoma and edema can distort MRI findings
To allow the radiologist to perform a CT-guided biopsy simultaneously
Because MRI contrast is contraindicated after a fresh surgical incision
items.e: MRI is the investigation of choice for local staging and should be done before biopsy because the hematoma and edema resulting from the biopsy can distort the MRI images, potentially overstating the tumor extent and complicating surgical planning.
items.note: This is a fundamental principle of musculoskeletal oncology staging sequence.

items.q: According to the AJCC 8th edition staging system for primary bone tumors of the appendicular skeleton, a tumor that presents with discontinuous 'skip lesions' in the primary bone is classified as which T category?
items.e: In the AJCC 8th edition for bone tumors, T1 is a tumor 8 cm or less, T2 is more than 8 cm, and T3 is defined by the presence of discontinuous tumors (skip lesions) in the primary bone.
items.note: Factually accurate according to the AJCC 8th edition staging criteria for bone.

items.q: A 22-year-old presents with a high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femur that has breached the cortex and involves the surrounding soft tissues, but shows no distant metastasis on PET-CT. What is the Enneking (MSTS) stage for this presentation?
items.e: Enneking Stage IIB represents a high-grade (G2), extracompartmental (T2) tumor without metastasis (M0). Since the tumor has breached the cortex into the soft tissues, it is extracompartmental. This is the most common stage at presentation for osteosarcoma.
items.note: Correct application of the Enneking staging system for malignant bone tumours.

items.q: Which of the following sarcomas is known for its propensity to spread to regional lymph nodes, necessitating lymph node assessment during staging?
items.e: Sarcomas that frequently spread to lymph nodes are remembered by the SCARE mnemonic: Synovial sarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, and Epithelioid sarcoma. Regional lymph node metastasis in Enneking staging is considered M1 (Stage III).
items.note: Tests the clinically important 'SCARE' mnemonic for nodal-spreading sarcomas.

items.q: A pathologist reviewing a resected osteosarcoma specimen after neoadjuvant chemotherapy uses the Huvos grading system. Which of the following findings classifies the patient as a 'good responder'?
o: Tumor necrosis of 90% or more (Grade III or IV)
Complete ossification of the tumor matrix
items.e: In the Huvos system, a 'good responder' is defined as having 90% or more tumor necrosis (Grade III: 90-99%; Grade IV: 100%). This is considered the strongest prognostic factor in non-metastatic osteosarcoma.
items.note: Correctly identifies the threshold for chemotherapy response in osteosarcoma.

items.q: Molecular analysis of a biopsy specimen from an epimetaphyseal lesion in a 30-year-old reveals an H3F3A (H3.3) G34W mutation. This finding is highly specific for:
items.e: The H3F3A G34W mutation is characteristic of Giant Cell Tumour (GCT) of bone. In contrast, chondroblastoma is typically associated with the H3F3B K36M mutation.
items.note: Tests high-yield molecular markers for common bone tumours.

items.q: A biopsy is requested for a painful, enlarging mass in the thigh of a young athlete. Radiographs show a 'zonal pattern' with mature peripheral ossification. Why is biopsy generally avoided in this 'don't touch' lesion?
o: It may cause a massive hematoma and compartment syndrome
The lesion is likely an avulsion fracture which heals with rest
The immature central proliferating cells can be misread as osteosarcoma
Biopsy will stimulate the lesion to undergo malignant transformation
items.e: The description fits Myositis Ossificans. Biopsy of the immature center of this lesion can be misread histologically as osteosarcoma. Diagnosis is best made by recognizing the zonal pattern of peripheral maturation on imaging.
items.note: Tests the classic 'don't touch' lesion pitfall in orthopaedic oncology.

items.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a persistent draining sinus from a femur fracture treated with an intramedullary nail 8 months ago. Radiographs show an infected nonunion with through-and-through cortical destruction, rendering the bone mechanically unstable. According to the Cierny-Mader classification, what is the anatomical stage?
items.e: Cierny-Mader Type IV (Diffuse) osteomyelitis involves through-and-through infection that is mechanically unstable either before or after debridement, such as an infected nonunion. Type III (Localised) is full-thickness but remains stable.
items.note: The question accurately tests the Cierny-Mader anatomical staging based on the provided notes and standard orthopaedic teaching.

items.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with pain and swelling of the first metatarsal head three days after stepping on a nail while wearing sneakers. Which organism is the most likely cause of osteochondritis in this specific setting?
items.e: While S. aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the characteristic organism associated with puncture wounds through the rubber soles of shoes (sneakers).
items.note: This is a classic 'exam pearl' regarding specific organisms in specific clinical settings, directly supported by the notes.

items.q: Which of the following is considered a 'confirmatory' criterion for the diagnosis of fracture-related infection (FRI) according to the 2018/2020 consensus definitions?
o: New or persistent wound drainage beyond the first few days
A single deep tissue culture positive for S. aureus
Presence of a fistula or sinus communicating with the bone or implant
items.e: Confirmatory criteria for FRI include a fistula/sinus communicating with bone/implant, purulent drainage/pus at surgery, indistinguishable pathogens in 2+ separate deep samples, or specific histopathology (>5 neutrophils/HPF). Wound drainage and single cultures are only 'suggestive' criteria.
items.note: The question correctly distinguishes between confirmatory and suggestive criteria as per the Metsemakers/Govaert consensus mentioned in the notes.

items.q: A 60-year-old patient with a 25-year history of chronic osteomyelitis of the tibia presents with a change in symptoms, including increased pain and a foul-smelling, bloody discharge from a long-standing sinus. Physical examination reveals a fungating mass with everted edges. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: A Marjolin ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma that develops in a long-standing chronic osteomyelitis sinus tract, typically after decades. Suspicious signs include everted edges, fungating masses, and bloody discharge.
items.note: The clinical presentation is classic for Marjolin ulcer, a high-yield topic in orthopaedic infection.

items.q: In the surgical management of chronic osteomyelitis, the Masquelet technique is often used for segmental bone defects. What is the primary role of the PMMA cement spacer in the first stage of this technique?
o: To induce a vascular membrane that secretes growth factors
To serve as a permanent scaffold for osteoconduction
items.e: The Masquelet (induced-membrane) technique involves a first stage where a PMMA spacer induces a vascular membrane. This membrane secretes growth factors (VEGF, TGF-beta, BMP-2) and is preserved during the second stage when the cavity is packed with autograft.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the biological principle of the Masquelet technique as described in the reference notes.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 'hot' swollen knee. Synovial fluid analysis reveals a white blood cell count of 85,000/mm³ with 92% neutrophils. Gram stain is negative. No crystals are seen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Start oral NSAIDs and review in 48 hours
Urgent joint drainage (arthroscopic or open) and empirical antibiotics
Wait for final culture results before initiating any treatment
items.e: A synovial WBC >50,000 and neutrophils >75-90% is highly suggestive of septic arthritis, which is an orthopaedic emergency. Management requires urgent joint drainage and empirical antibiotics after sampling.
items.note: The question tests the diagnostic threshold and emergency management of septic arthritis.

items.q: On T1-weighted MRI, a rim of slightly higher signal intensity (granulation tissue) lining an abscess cavity in the metaphysis of a long bone is known as the:
items.e: The 'penumbra sign' on T1-weighted MRI is a rim of granulation tissue with slightly higher signal than the abscess itself. It is characteristic of subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess) and helps distinguish it from tumours.
items.note: The penumbra sign is a specific radiological hallmark mentioned in the notes for subacute osteomyelitis.

items.q: A 25-year-old male presents with migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrist, and painless pustular skin lesions on his hands. What is the most likely causative organism for this clinical triad?
items.e: The triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis (painless pustules), and migratory polyarthralgia is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection, the most common cause of septic arthritis in healthy, sexually active young adults.
items.note: This is a classic clinical triad for gonococcal arthritis, which is the most common cause of septic arthritis in healthy, sexually active young adults.

items.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with a limp and pain in the right hip. On examination, the limb is held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation. There is an apparent lengthening of 2 cm, but the true lengths are equal. According to the stages described by Tuli and Babhulkar, what is the most likely radiological finding at this stage?
o: Significant narrowing of the joint space
Haziness of the articular margins and juxta-articular osteopenia
Marginal erosions with reduced joint space
items.e: The clinical attitude of flexion, abduction, and external rotation with apparent lengthening defines Stage I (Synovitis) of hip tuberculosis. Radiologically, this stage shows only soft tissue haziness and osteopenia; the joint space is typically preserved or even slightly increased due to effusion.
items.note: The question accurately maps the clinical stage of hip TB to its radiological features as per the Tuli/Babhulkar classification.

items.q: A patient undergoing treatment for knee tuberculosis with a first-line daily fixed-dose combination regimen (HRZE) presents with acute pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Laboratory investigations reveal a serum uric acid level of 9.2 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of this complication?
items.e: Pyrazinamide is known to cause hyperuricaemia and clinical gout by inhibiting the renal excretion of uric acid. It is also considered the most hepatotoxic of the first-line antitubercular drugs.
items.note: This is a classic pharmacology-orthopaedic crossover question regarding ATT side effects.

items.q: The 'triple deformity' of the knee seen in advanced tuberculous arthritis consists of which of the following combinations of tibial displacement relative to the femur?
o: Flexion, posterior subluxation, and internal rotation
Flexion, posterior subluxation, and external rotation
Extension, anterior subluxation, and external rotation
Flexion, anterior subluxation, and internal rotation
items.e: In advanced knee TB, destruction of ligaments and muscle contractures (hamstrings and ITB) lead to the 'triple deformity': flexion, posterior subluxation of the tibia, and external rotation of the tibia (often with valgus).
items.note: The triple deformity is a hallmark of advanced knee TB and is correctly described in the options.

items.q: A 35-year-old female presents with a chronic, dumbbell-shaped swelling extending from the distal forearm to the palm. She demonstrates 'cross-fluctuation' above and below the flexor retinaculum. Surgical exploration is likely to reveal which pathognomonic finding?
o: Haemosiderin-laden synovium with blooming on MRI
Bony sequestra within the carpal bones
items.e: The clinical description of a dumbbell-shaped swelling with cross-fluctuation is classic for a compound palmar ganglion (tuberculous tenosynovitis of the flexor sheaths). This condition is frequently associated with the presence of 'melon-seed' or 'rice' bodies within the synovial sheath.
items.note: The clinical presentation and pathognomonic finding are accurately linked.

items.q: According to the 2021 WHO definitions, a patient with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) who also shows resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one of bedaquiline or linezolid is classified as having:
items.e: The 2021 WHO definition of Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (XDR-TB) is MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to a fluoroquinolone and at least one 'Group A' drug (bedaquiline or linezolid). Pre-XDR is defined as MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone.
items.note: The question tests the most recent and relevant WHO definitions for drug resistance.

items.q: A 50-year-old male presents with marked wasting of the right shoulder girdle and painful restriction of all movements. Radiographs show significant erosions of the humeral head and glenoid, but there is a notable absence of cold abscesses or sinus formation. This 'dry' form of tuberculosis is known as:
items.e: Caries sicca is the dry, atrophic form of tuberculosis typically seen in the shoulder. It is characterized by marked muscle wasting and painful stiffness (mimicking frozen shoulder) but lacks the classic 'cold abscess' or pus formation seen in other sites.
items.note: Caries sicca is a specific eponym for shoulder TB that is frequently tested.

items.q: In the Shanmugasundaram radiological classification of hip tuberculosis, which of the following types is associated with the best clinical prognosis?
items.e: The Shanmugasundaram classification describes various radiological patterns of hip TB. The 'normal-looking' and 'Perthes-like' types carry the best prognosis for a functional joint, whereas types like 'travelling acetabulum' or 'atrophic' indicate more severe destruction.
items.note: The classification and its prognostic implications are correctly identified.

items.q: What is the primary pathological reason why the joint space is typically preserved until late stages in tuberculous arthritis, unlike pyogenic arthritis?
o: Tuberculous bacilli produce inhibitors of matrix metalloproteinases
The tuberculous pannus lacks the abundant proteolytic enzymes found in pyogenic infections
Early fibrous ankylosis stabilizes the cartilage
The high acid pH of the joint fluid protects the articular cartilage
items.e: Tuberculosis is characterized by a relatively slow destruction of cartilage because the tuberculous granulation tissue (pannus) contains fewer proteolytic enzymes compared to the aggressive purulent exudate seen in pyogenic infections. Thus, joint space narrowing is a late feature in TB (Phemister triad).
items.note: This tests the fundamental pathological difference between TB and pyogenic arthritis.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with short stature and significant genu varum. Laboratory investigation reveals a low serum phosphate level and high alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels are within the normal range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH) is characterized by low phosphate due to renal wasting (FGF23 excess) but typically presents with normal serum calcium and normal or only slightly elevated PTH, unlike calcipenic forms where PTH is markedly high.
items.note: The biochemistry (low PO4, normal Ca, normal PTH) is the classic differentiator for XLH in entrance exams.

items.q: An adult patient with chronic malabsorption presents with diffuse bone pain and a waddling gait. Radiographs show narrow lucent bands perpendicular to the cortex on the medial femoral neck and the axillary border of the scapula. These findings are most accurately described as:
items.e: Looser zones (pseudofractures) are characteristic of osteomalacia. They are narrow lucent bands of unmineralised osteoid typically located on the concave (medial/compression) side of bones, such as the medial femoral neck and axillary border of the scapula.
items.note: The description of the location (medial femoral neck, axillary scapula) and morphology is classic for Looser zones.

items.q: In the pathophysiology of rickets, the primary failure of mineralisation and subsequent widening of the physis occurs specifically within which zone of the growth plate?
items.e: Rickets is specifically a disease of the hypertrophic zone. Low phosphate prevents the apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes, causing the hypertrophic zone to widen and the zone of provisional calcification to fail to mineralise.
items.note: This is a fundamental pathological fact frequently tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 2-year-old child with severe rickets is found to have very high serum levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). On examination, the child also has total scalp alopecia. What is the most likely underlying defect?
items.e: Vitamin D dependent rickets (VDDR) Type 2 is caused by a vitamin D receptor defect. It is characterized by high PTH, low calcium, and uniquely very high levels of calcitriol (due to end-organ resistance) and is frequently associated with alopecia.
items.note: The combination of high calcitriol and alopecia is the classic 'spotter' for VDDR Type 2.

items.q: A 6-year-old girl with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH) has failed to show significant improvement on conventional therapy with oral phosphate and calcitriol. Which of the following is now considered the first-line medical treatment for improving rickets severity and growth in such cases?
items.e: Burosumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody against FGF23. In clinical trials, it has shown greater efficacy in improving rickets severity, growth, and phosphate levels in children with XLH compared to conventional therapy.
items.note: Burosumab is the most significant recent advancement in rickets management and is a high-yield topic.

items.q: A child presents with clinical and radiological features of rickets and a history of early loss of deciduous teeth with intact roots. Laboratory results show normal serum calcium and phosphate, but a significantly low serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Hypophosphatasia is an inherited disorder caused by ALPL mutations. It presents with rickets-like changes but is distinguished by very low ALP levels and premature loss of deciduous teeth.
items.note: Low ALP in a rickets-like presentation is the defining feature of hypophosphatasia.

items.q: A 3-year-old child with nutritional rickets has significant genu varum. What is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this deformity?
o: Medical management with vitamin D and calcium
items.e: Medical control of the metabolic disease is the first priority. Most bowing in nutritional rickets remodels spontaneously within 1-2 years after starting vitamin D and calcium treatment; surgery is only indicated if deformity persists after metabolic control.
items.note: Emphasizes the core principle of 'metabolic control before surgery' in rickets.

items.q: Which of the following radiological findings is considered pathognomonic for secondary hyperparathyroidism in a patient with renal osteodystrophy?
o: Subperiosteal resorption on the radial side of middle phalanges
items.e: Subperiosteal resorption on the radial side of the middle phalanges is a pathognomonic radiological sign of hyperparathyroidism, often seen in the context of renal osteodystrophy.
items.note: This is a classic 'pathognomonic' fact found in Campbell's and standard radiology texts.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a five‑day history of painful swelling and erythema of the great toe. Synovial fluid reveals 4,500 WBC/mm³, predominantly neutrophils, and needle‑shaped, negatively birefringent crystals under compensated polarised light. Which of the following is the most appropriate first‑line treatment for this acute flare in a patient with normal renal function and no contraindication to NSAIDs?
items.e: In an acute gout flare with no contraindications, NSAIDs are the preferred first‑line therapy. Colchicine and steroids are alternatives, and IL‑1 blockers are reserved for refractory cases.
items.note: Conforms with current guidelines; all other options are correct but not first‑line.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man with a long history of alcohol intake and recurrent episodes of inflammatory knee pain is found to have a serum urate of 9.2 mg/dL. Which of the following laboratory values is most likely to be normal during an acute gout flare?
items.e: During an acute flare, the serum urate level can fall because of inflammation; it is the lab test most likely to be deceptively normal or even low.
items.note: Accurate reflection of clinical pathophysiology.

items.q: In a patient with chronic tophaceous gout, a soft‑tissue swelling over the Achilles tendon shows a heterogeneously enhancing area on MRI and surrounding edema. Which of the following statements best describes the most common complication of a large tophus in this location?
o: Tumour‑like mass effect on the nerve
Compression of the tibial nerve leading to weakness
items.e: Tophi over the Achilles tendon frequently lead to tendon rupture due to the mechanical bearing of the mass on the tendinous structure.
items.note: Consistent with clinical data on Achilles tophi.

items.q: A 38‑year‑old woman presents with acute severe left knee pain after a night out. Synovial fluid demonstrates 8,000 WBC/mm³ and needle‑shaped crystals. Which of the following is the most important reason to still send the fluid for Gram stain and culture?
o: To confirm the presence of crystals
To determine the type of crystal
items.e: Crystals can coexist with infection; if septic arthritis is present, wrong treatment can result. Hence Gram stain and culture are mandatory.
items.note: Reflects standard infectious precautions.
items.reason: repeats ai20261119_040 in this batch (crystals do not exclude sepsis)

items.q: Which of the following is a characteristic radiographic finding of chronic gout that distinguishes it from rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Juxta‑articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
items.e: Chronic gout shows “punched‑out” juxta‑articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign), whereas RA shows periarticular osteopenia and symmetric joint space narrowing.
items.note: Clear, evidence‑based imaging feature.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old man presents with deep, constant pain in the left femur that worsens at night. X‑ray shows an antero‑laterally bowed femur with a sharp, sub‑tangential cortical line that looks like a "blade of grass" on the medial side. Which phase of Paget disease is most likely active in this region?
items.e: The classic "blade of grass" lytic front indicates the osteoclast‑driven lytic phase of Paget disease.
items.note: Facts match Campbell and note

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with long‑standing polyostotic Paget disease reports sudden deafness. Which of the following is the most plausible explanation?
o: Compression of cranial nerves by basilar invagination
Diffuse hyperostosis of the otic capsule
items.e: Diffuse hyperostosis of the otic capsule (option D) best explains sudden sensorineural/ conductive deafness characteristic of Paget. Basilar invagination causes cranial nerve palsies but not abrupt deafness.
items.note: Correct answer was mis‑stated; corrected to true option

items.q: Which laboratory finding is most specific for active Paget disease in a patient with raised alkaline phosphatase?
items.e: Urinary hydroxyproline is a resorption marker that rises with active osteoclastic activity in Paget disease.
items.note: Board sources accept urinary hydroxyproline as the best resorption marker
items.reason: repeats cmwlsx1tu24kif (most specific lab in active Paget)

items.q: A 45‑year‑old male physician who has worked in a poultry farm reports a sudden increase in his serum alkaline phosphatase and normal calcium and phosphate. He has no bone pain. Imaging shows a single enlarged humerus with a "candle flame" lytic front. Which of the following is the most appropriate first‑line treatment?
items.e: Zoledronic acid is the preferred bisphosphonate for active Paget disease and offers sustained suppression of bone turnover.
items.note: Consistent with Campbell & NICE guidelines

items.q: When planning a surgical procedure on a patient with extensive Paget disease of the femur, which intraoperative complication is most feared?
o: Inadequate implant fixation due to poor bone quality
items.e: Pagetic bone is highly vascular with arteriovenous shunts, making uncontrolled intra‑operative bleeding a major risk.
items.note: Widely reported in orthopaedic literature

items.q: Which radiographic sign is characteristic of a Pagetic skull and is used to distinguish it from osteoblastic metastasis?
items.e: The "cotton‑wool" calcification pattern is typical of Paget disease; osteoblastic metastases show more uniform dense sclerosis.
items.note: Classic imaging feature

items.q: A 38‑year‑old man presents with insidious groin pain; he has been on high‑dose oral prednisolone (60 mg/day) for a flare of lupus for the last 4 months. Plain radiographs are normal. Which investigation is most appropriate to detect early osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: MRI is the most sensitive (≈99 %) for early, pre‑radiographic disease and will reveal the characteristic T1 low‑signal band and T2 double‑line sign.
items.note: All facts stated in notes.
items.reason: repeats cai20261107_006 / cai20261109_012 (MRI for early ON)

items.q: An 11‑year‑old girl with sickle cell disease presents with sudden onset groin pain. She has no history of trauma. Which factor is the most likely direct cause of her osteonecrosis?
o: Sickle‑cell sickling within femoral head vessels
items.e: In sickle cell disease, sickle‑cell sickling of marrow vessels causes intravascular occlusion and focal ischaemia of the femoral head.
items.note: Sickling is the established pathophysiology.

items.q: During evaluation of a patient with bilateral osteonecrosis of the femoral heads, imaging shows a crescent sign on the frog‑leg lateral radiograph. Which statement best describes the significance of this finding?
o: It confirms necrosis is limited to the femoral neck
items.e: The crescent sign represents a subchondral fracture and is the radiological marker that the necrotic zone is about to collapse.
items.note: Definition matches standard teaching.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old alcoholic presents with right hip pain. MRI shows a necrotic zone occupying 30 % of the femoral head area and extending mainly medially. According to the ARCO staging, what is the most appropriate early treatment?
items.e: ARCO stage I/II (necrotic area >25 % but <50 % and no collapse) is best managed with core decompression to relieve intra‑osseous pressure.
items.note: ARCO criteria and treatment ladder are standard.

items.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease on methotrexate and high serum lipoprotein(a) has multifocal osteonecrosis involving the femoral heads and shoulders. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely contributing to his disease?
items.e: Hyperlipidaemia (high lipoprotein(a)) promotes fat emboli and intra‑osseous fat deposition, both predisposing to osteonecrosis.
items.note: Lab abnormality matches known pathogenesis.

items.q: A 12‑year‑old boy with a physeal injury now presents with a growth arrest callus. Which signaling pathway disruption is most likely responsible for the formation of such an arrest callus?
items.e: Growth plate arrest is classically due to loss of Wnt/β‑catenin signaling in osteoblast lineage cells; the pathway is essential for osteoblast differentiation (RUNX2‑osteoblast axis).
items.note: All facts are corroborated by the reference notes.

items.q: Which of the following molecules is a bone‑specific marker released from the plasma membrane of osteoblasts and is increased in bone formation?
items.e: Alkaline phosphatase is a membrane‑bound enzyme of osteoblasts; it hydrolyses pyrophosphate to allow mineralisation and is a classical formation marker.
items.note: Matches standard orthopaedic physiology.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old farmer presents with progressive knee pain and radiographs show a smooth, horizontal line across the cartilage surface that runs parallel to the articular surface. This line represents the:
items.e: The tidemark marks the interface between uncalcified and calcified cartilage; it is a basophilic line seen on histology and radiographs.
items.note: Correct as stated.

items.q: Which proteoglycan is predominantly responsible for the osmotic swelling pressure that gives articular cartilage its load‑bearing resistance?
items.e: Aggrecan carries large GAG chains (chondroitin and keratan sulfate) that attract water via the Donnan effect, producing compressive stiffness.
items.note: Correct as stated.

items.q: Which of the following collagen subtypes is not usually found in the uncalcified zones of articular cartilage?
items.e: Type X collagen is expressed only in the calcified cartilage zone and hypertrophic physeal chondrocytes, not in the uncalcified cartilage.
items.note: Correct as stated.
items.reason: repeats cai20261120_088 (type X collagen in calcified cartilage)

items.q: In microfracture surgery for a full‑thickness cartilage defect, why is it essential that the drill holes penetrate into the calcified cartilage?
o: To allow bone bleeding into the defect
To achieve a thicker biological graft
items.e: Access to the marrow in the calcified zone supplies mesenchymal cells that fill the defect with fibrocartilaginous repair tissue.
items.note: Correct as stated.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old patient with osteopenic bone is being planned for a femoral stem arthroplasty. Which material property most explains the choice of a titanium alloy stem over a cobalt‑chrome alloy?
items.e: Titanium’s modulus (~110 GPa) is closest to cortical bone (~15–20 GPa), which reduces stress shielding compared with the much stiffer cobalt‑chrome alloy.
items.note: Correct – modulus proximity to bone explains the choice; the other options are unrelated to stress‑shielding.
items.reason: repeats today's written titanium modulus question

items.q: During a rotational high‑energy fracture of the tibial shaft, which fracture pattern is most consistent with the mechanism described in the notes?
items.e: Torsional loading generates a spiral fracture running along a 45‑degree helix.
items.note: Mechanism‑pattern mapping confirms spiral for torsion.

items.q: Which of the following statements about implant fatigue is TRUE according to the notes?
o: Fatigue failure occurs only once the ultimate tensile strength is exceeded;
The endurance limit is the stress below which an implant survives infinitely many cycles;
Notch sensitivity is irrelevant in titanium implants;
A scratch on a stainless‑steel plate has no effect on fatigue life
items.e: Fatigue failure occurs under repetitive loading below ultimate strength; the endurance limit defines the stress below which infinite cycles are tolerated.
items.note: Only statement B aligns with the notes.

items.q: A 24‑year‑old soccer player sustains a distal femoral shaft fracture with a transverse cleaved surface on the lateral cortex. Which loading scenario best explains this picture?
items.e: Bending with axial compression produces a transverse fracture with a butterfly fragment on the compression (concave) side.
items.note: Pattern matches bending mechanics.

items.q: Which characteristic of articular cartilage makes it the least stiff material listed in the relative modulus table?
o: Its lowest modulus in the MPa range;
items.e: Articular cartilage has the lowest modulus (MPa), making it the least stiff material.
items.note: Lowest modulus defines its stiffness.

items.q: A triangular cortical bone defect in a femoral shaft reduces torsional strength by:
items.e: Open‑section defects reduce torsional strength drastically, by up to ~90 %.
items.note: Bulleted note explicitly states up to ~90 %.

items.q: Which viscoelastic property of bone contributes to the observation that faster loading increases bone stiffness?
items.e: Under faster loading, bone behaves stiffer because the viscoelastic time‑dependent modulus increases with loading rate.
items.note: Rate‑dependent modulus is the cited mechanism.

items.q: A 12‑year‑old boy presents with a rapidly enlarging painful mass over the left distal femur. X‑ray shows a permeative lysis with an onion‑skin periosteal reaction. Core biopsy demonstrates sheets of small blue cells; immunostain is strongly membranous CD99 positive. Which genetic test confirms the diagnosis?
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is confirmed by demonstrating the EWSR1‑FLI1 fusion by FISH or RT‑PCR. The other options are specific to APL, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma and desmosarcoma.
items.note: Correct answer directly matches Ewing pathology

items.q: Which of the following is the most characteristic immunohistochemical marker for a primary lymphoma of bone?
items.e: Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma shows strong CD45 and CD20 expression; CD99 is typical of Ewing, CD138 for myeloma, and synaptophysin for neuroendocrine tumours.
items.note: Only CD45 is specific for lymphoma

items.q: A 6‑year‑old child has a diffuse abdominal mass and elevated serum LDH. Histology reveals Homer‑Wright rosettes. Neuroblastoma cytogenetics shows MYCN amplification. What is the implication of MYCN amplification?
o: It indicates a good response to chemotherapy
It is associated with poor outcome
It is only seen in metastatic disease
items.e: MYCN amplification is a recognised high‑risk feature in neuroblastoma, correlating with aggressive behaviour and poorer survival.
items.note: Standard prognostic fact

items.q: A 28‑year‑old man has a solitary lytic lesion of the humerus. Core biopsy shows small blue cells positive for CD99 and negative for CD45. Molecular testing shows a CIC‑DUX4 fusion. This tumour belongs to which group?
o: CIC‑Dux4 sarcoma, an Ewing‑like round cell sarcoma
items.e: CIC‑DUX4 sarcomas are Ewing‑like round cell tumours that are CD99 positive but do not have the classic EWSR1‑FLI1 translocation; they form a separate entity.
items.note: Genetic hallmark is unmistakable

items.q: Which of the following genetic alterations is characteristic of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma?
items.e: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma harbours PAX3‑FOXO1 or PAX7‑FOXO1 fusions; the other translocations are seen in Ewing, follicular lymphoma, and multiple myeloma respectively.
items.note: Classic genetic signature

items.q: A 55‑year‑old male presents with a painless, 8 cm deep mass in the mid‑thigh that has grown steadily over 4 months. MRI shows a heterogeneous tumour with central necrosis and a peritumoural oedema. Which imaging feature would most strongly argue against a high‑grade soft‑tissue sarcoma?
o: A thick, well‑defined fatty septa >2 mm
B central necrosis with peripheral contrast enhancement
D an infiltrative margin into surrounding muscle

items.q: A 63‑year‑old woman with chronic renal failure (eGFR 30 mL/min) develops joint pain. Synovial fluid WBC is 45,000/mm³, crystals are absent on microscopy, but Gram stain is negative. Which investigation is the best next step to rule out septic arthritis?

items.q: In calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) the crystals are best described as:
o: Needle‑shaped, strongly negatively birefringent, yellow when parallel

Tiny clumps, non‑birefringent, stain with alizarin red S
Flat plates, not birefringent, seen only in electron microscopy
items.e: CPPD crystals are rhomboid or rod‑shaped, weakly positively birefringent and appear blue when aligned parallel to the compensator axis.
items.note: Standard textbook description

items.q: A 48‑year‑old man with intermittent ankle pain is found to have chronic tophaceous gout. Which skeletal finding is most characteristic on plain radiograph of the affected joint?

Destructive punched‑out erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
Bilateral symmetrical erosions of carpal joints
Uniform subchondral cysts with no erosions
items.e: Chronic gout produces classic “punched‑out” juxta‑articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign).

items.q: Mutations in which transcription factor are the cause of cleidocranial dysplasia?

items.q: Which osteocyte‑derived protein acts as a systemic inhibitor of bone formation by antagonising Wnt signalling?

items.q: During a joint arthroscopy, the surgeon notes a faint brown line at the interface of uncalcified and calcified cartilage. Which anatomical structure does this line represent?

items.q: A patient undergoes a microfracture procedure for a full‑thickness cartilage defect. To maximise the chance of reparative tissue filling the defect, the surgeon should:
